# Ring of Nestor

The Ring of Nestor is the name commonly given to a gold signet ring that entered scholarly literature in 1925 and became associated with interpretations of Minoan imagery and the afterlife. Sir Arthur Evans published a 1925 study titled *The Ring of Nestor: A Glimpse into the Minoan After-World and a Sepulchral Treasure of Gold Signet-Rings and Bead-Seals from Thisbe, Boeotia*. The ring’s reported discovery in 1924 and its association with a tholos tomb at Kakovatos near Pylos are not supported in the supplied material by a professionally documented excavation record. Its authenticity has received conflicting assessments: Evans accepted it and used its imagery in a Minoan afterlife interpretation, while members of the archaeological board in Athens reportedly rejected it as a modern forgery. A later peer-reviewed article by Nanno Marinatos and Briana Jackson argued that the ring’s butterfly motif weighs against authenticity, although the available abstract does not provide the full iconographic analysis. The reported Kakovatos find context is therefore not equivalent to verified provenance, and the opposing historical assessments do not establish a settled authentication result. These questions place the object within the category *gemma dubitanda*, a technical term for sealstones and signet rings attributed to the Aegean Bronze Age whose provenance is not securely documented.

## Description and reported provenance

The ring is a gold signet ring with an engraved bezel. The supplied sources identify an illustration of it as “Ring of Nestor. CMS VI, 277,” while another record documents Evans’s drawing and a watercolour associated with the object. The ring’s commonly used name derives from its reported association with the Pylos region, identified in the sources with the legendary home of Nestor.

A 2019 study describes the ring as allegedly discovered in a tholos tomb at Kakovatos near Pylos and records its first appearance in scholarly literature in 1925. The same study states that Evans privately purchased the object and published it in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*, whereas members of the archaeological board in Athens had previously refused to buy it because they considered it a forgery made by a modern artist. The discovery account therefore belongs to the object’s reported history rather than to a securely verified excavation provenance. In the study’s discussion of *gemmae dubitandae*, the absence of professional, well-documented archaeological excavations is given as a reason for withholding confidence in Bronze Age attribution.

## Iconography and interpretation

The ring’s bezel carries a miniature engraved scene. Evans interpreted the pictorial composition as a Minoan Elysian domain in which a human couple journeys to the Beyond and enters the Elysian Fields. In that reading, butterflies and chrysalises could symbolize the human soul; a later account of Evans’s interpretation connects the soul with weighing and possible reincarnation. These are historical interpretations attributed to Evans, not an independently established reconstruction of Minoan religious belief.

The object is catalogued as CMS VI, no. 277. A 2020 study identifies a pictorial unit previously called Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon” as a scorpion and interprets it as an apotropaic figure that kills the ring’s “Minoan Dragon.” Because the accessible material supplies the study’s abstract but not its complete visual analysis, this identification should be treated as that study’s interpretation rather than as an uncontested description. The available record documents Evans’s drawing, a colour watercolour, and comparisons with other imagery, but the supplied excerpts do not provide the full arguments attached to those illustrations.

## Authenticity debate

The authenticity question was present from the object’s first documented scholarly circulation. A source states that the ring was found in 1924 and that Arthur Evans accepted it as authentic, whereas many other scholars condemned it as a forgery. A more specific account reports that members of the archaeological board in Athens refused to buy it because they considered it “a forgery manufactured by a modern artist”; Evans nevertheless privately purchased it and published it in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*. These were conflicting historical assessments: the board’s judgment and Evans’s publication document opposing positions, but neither fact by itself establishes the object’s modern or Bronze Age manufacture.

Arguments against authenticity include the suspicious circumstances of the reported discovery and the lack of a professionally documented excavation provenance. Marinatos and Jackson further argue that the ring’s interpretive coherence depends on Egyptian prototypes and that its butterfly motif weighs against authenticity; the supplied text provides their abstract-level conclusion but not the detailed comparisons. The term *gemma dubitanda* captures this evidentiary position: it refers to sealstones and signet rings attributed to the Aegean Bronze Age whose provenance and authenticity remain uncertain.

The dispute has not been uniform across later writing. The supplied abstract of a 2020 study states that earlier identifications of certain gold rings, including the Ring of Nestor, were reassessed in favour of authenticity on the basis of comparable iconographic finds and more detailed study of technique and craftsmanship. The available material therefore records a later pro-authenticity reassessment alongside continuing uncertainty about the ring’s provenance and manufacture; it does not establish a settled authentication result.

## Abstract

TO-DAY even the most old-fashioned admirer of Hellenism has to admit that classical Greek civilisation was not only preceded by but also actually rooted in the Minoan culture of Crete and its continental daughter, the Mycenaean. The excavator of Minos' palace at Knossos, who so dramatically found the key to the riddle of pre-classical Greece, has himself taken the lead in tracing the influence of the Minoan civilisation on the classical; again and again he has illuminated the dark background of Hellenic life by a reference to the remains of the prehistoric age or interpreted the monuments of that still dumb epoch from the records of historic Greece.

The Ring of Nestor: a Glimpse into the Minoan After-World and a Sepulchral Treasure of Gold Signet-Rings and Bead-Seals from Thisbe, Boeotia.

## Abstract

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

When Malcolm Wiener stated in his article that “jewelry above all is subject to the dictates of style and to the Versailles effect” (Wiener 1984, 24), he referred to the “Versailles effect” as an effect “most likely to occur where the cultural prestige of one society within an interconnecting set of societies is great” (Wiener 1984, 17). He pointed out that besides pottery ‒ frequently used for tracing movements of goods or even groups of people ‒ jewelry too has a high potential to illustrate intercultural patterns of commercial, political or ideological exchange. In doing so the “Versailles effect” does not implicate the simple imitation of the material culture of another, (dominant) culture by force or political /military domination, but rather describes a voluntary adaption to this culture, mostly expressed through art forms as well as pottery styles, architectural features or even technological inventions (Wiener 2016, 1-2). In this paper the focus will be laid on a quite similar effect here called the “Knossos effect”, made visible by an examination of distribution patterns of golden signets and their chronology. The term is a reference to Wiener’s term and is used here to describe a similar phenomenon “spreading” from the palace of Knossos in LM IA Crete.

This paper addresses the cultural translation of some exotica – selected valuable objects that were brought from the south Aegean or even more distant areas to Troy, Beşik-Tepe and Greek Macedonia mainly during the Late Bronze Age. The discussion will focus on jewellery and seals made of carnelian, steatite and bone. Such foreign goods, often labelled as imports, are usually objects with complicated histories. These histories began with acquisition, then went through various forms of ownership and display, and finally ended with release, all while simultaneously undergoing a process of domestication and 'de-exotification'. Release, especially an intentional release such as in the case of burial goods, treasures and cult deposits, is discussed comprehensively since these are the best-documented cases of interaction between things and people in the area of the north Aegean. Also discussed is the phenomenon of copying as a complicated procedure of appropriation, as well as the case of rejection of ornaments and symbolism.

In this paper I discuss the connection between the double axe and bulls. The double axe was undoubtedly one of the most important religious symbols in Minoan Crete. There is, however, no general consensus regarding its meaning. That the double axe was associated with the sacrifice of bulls and used to kill or to stun the animal was first suggested by Martin P. Nilsson in 1950 and probably still remains the most common interpretation, although perhaps more by default than for any other reasons. This interpretation is not implausible since the sacrifice of bulls would seem to have been part of Minoan ritual as documented by the iconographical evidence, most notably on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus. Moreover, the figures carrying large double axes with a definite air of purpose that are depicted on a number of seals could plausibly be identified as sacrificial priests and priestesses (eg. CMS II.6, no.10). The interpretation of the double axe as a sacrificial implement has all the same been questioned, not least because we have no depictions showing it actually being used as such. The double axes depicted on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus seem to be symbols rather than cult equipment, but this may be debatable. The iconographical evidence clearly indicates that there was some kind of symbolic connection between the double axe and bulls, whether this was related to sacrifice or not. Mention can be made of a number of seals which show a bull’s head with a double axe between the horns (eg. CMS II.3, no.11). The same motif also occurs on pottery. In most examples it is only the head of the animal which is depicted in connection with the double axe. The symbolic value of the double axe would seem to have been particularly associated with the head and perhaps specifically with the horns of the animal. It is noticeable that the horns can be shown in many different ways. The use of axes to shape the horns of cattle is widely attested in eastern African. The axes that are used in this process acquire exceptional symbolic value. This practice has an attested long time-depth and it is believed that it can be traced far back into prehistory and significantly in this context, it seems to be documented in ancient Egyptian iconography. That part of the symbolic meaning of the double axe in Minoan Crete could derive from its use in manipulating the horns of living bulls into a desirable shape is a possible interpretation of the iconographical evidence, which may also be supported by osteological evidence. In the last part of my paper I discuss the iconographical evidence for the association between bulls and double axes in terms of ritual meaning and cosmological beliefs.

The Bronze Age Aegean lacks a clearly discernible iconography of rulership, permitting widely contrasting speculation on the character of Minoan society; that it was egalitarian, heterarchical, gynocratic or a theocracy overseen by priest-kings. That elites did exist is amply attested through mortuary, iconographic and architectural evidence including the Throne Room of the Late Minoan palace at Knossos in which a centrally-oriented throne is incorporated into the architectural fabric of the room. Frescoes adorn the wall into which the throne is set, griffins flanking its large, mountain-shaped seat-back. Iconographic representations of human figures holding sceptres and standing upon mountains, and evidence for the increased palatial control of cultic activity at rural peak sanctuaries during the Neopalatial period (1750–1490 B.C.E.) emphasise an association between rulership and the mountainous landscape. It will be argued that literal and metaphoric representations of a mountain throne function within an ideological program associating rulership with the natural landscape, offering new insights into the construction of power in the Aegean Bronze Age.----------- Paper presented at the 10th International Congress on the Archaeology of the Ancient Near East (ICAANE) on 27 April 2016.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.

Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

## [July 2011 (115.3)](https://ajaonline.org/toc/1153/)
#### Book Review

# Corpus der minoischen und mykenischen Siegel. Vol. 6, Oxford, the Ashmolean Museum

By Helen Hughes-Brock

Reviewed by [Olga Krzyszkowska](https://ajaonline.org/author/2217/)

[Read Article](https://doi.org/10.3764/ajaonline1153.Krzyszkowska)

The publication of any volume of the _Corpus der minoischen und mykenischen Siegel_ (_CMS_) is welcome; the long-awaited appearance of the sixth volume of _CMS_ is a cause for celebration, for this presents the priceless collection of 516 Aegean Bronze Age seals housed in the Ashmolean Museum (sealings and subsequent purchases from private collections appear in _CMS_ 2, nos. 7, 8; _CMS_ 8; _CMS_ 10; concordances 39, 40).

Essential reading is the foreword (ix–x) by the series editor, Ingo Pini, setting out the long gestation of the Oxford volume. The project was originally assigned to Kenna, following his publication _Cretan Seals_ (Oxford 1960). After Kenna’s death, Boardman prepared the catalogue descriptions; in 1978, the mantle passed to Hughes-Brock. Most photographs of seals and casts were executed almost 50 years ago by Albiker, using highly unsatisfactory techniques. The results, despite much enhancing of the scans by Pini himself, are decidedly variable. The casts themselves are also variable in quality, made in plaster, Vinagel, silicone, and plasticine. Not widely recognized (even by photographers) is that each material demands specific lighting techniques. For certain important pieces, new plasticine impressions were made and photographed by Pini; excellent drawings were prepared by the _CMS_ draftsman Lieberknecht (others are less good; credits appear on pp. xi–xii). Catalogue order and all-important dating was determined by Pini (51); much advice on materials and techniques was proffered by Müller.

Hughes-Brock’s introduction covers the history and sources of the collection (3–29); find places and places of acquisition on Crete; materials and shapes; manufacture and technology; motif, iconography, and style; and objects not in the catalogue. Also preceding the catalogue proper is a valuable appendix summarizing scientific analyses of selected pieces (31–5); concordances and indices follow (37–51). Comments below are perforce highly selective.

A substantial number of the Oxford seals belonged to Arthur Evans; many were acquired during his travels across the island in the 1890s. Places of acquisition, documented in his notebooks, are generally more trustworthy than those given in _Scripta Minoa_ (vol. 1 [Oxford 1909]), _Palace of Minos_(4 vols. [London 1921–1935]), or _Cretan Seals_. An especially happy piece of detective work now links number 104, the famous Middle Minoan (MM) II hieroglyphic prism that first aroused Evans’ interest in Crete, to Lakónia (Mirabello) and not Lakonía (Sparta). Admittedly, such information cannot be construed as provenance in the strict archaeological sense, yet it can offer valuable insights into distribution patterns. Even in the Herakleion Museum, a high proportion of the seals are little more than stray finds.

Hughes-Brock rightly stresses the difficulties of identifying materials, especially the soft stones used extensively for Cretan seals (chlorite, steatite, serpentine). Since changing patterns of use may reflect chronological or regional factors, accuracy is important. While identifications here are markedly better than in _Cretan Seals_, some individual pieces and groups will certainly merit reexamination in future. Number 84, published in _Cretan Seals_ (no. 102) as “steatite” and here as “serpentine” (an unlikely material for MM I–II), is surely chlorite: the piece belongs to the recently identified Mesara-Chlorite Group, datable a trifle earlier than the steatite prisms of east Crete (M. Anastasiadou, _The Middle Minoan Three-Sided Soft Stone Prism: A Study of Style and Iconography. CMS_ Beiheft 9 [2011] 127–28, no. 503).

MM II steatite prisms (nos. 26–90) account for about 10% of the Oxford collection, reflecting Evans’ interest in “pictographic” seals. Most sit easily in the Malia/east Cretan group identified by Anastasiadou: production is linked closely to the seal-cutter’s workshop at Malia Quartier Mu. Contemporary output in hard semiprecious stones (e.g., agate, carnelian, chalcedony, jasper) includes justly famous prisms (nos. 91–106), _Petschafte_ (nos. 124, 125, 127–34), and zoomorphic seals and foliate backs (nos. 138–49). Most bear fine figural motifs and/or hieroglyphic inscriptions, though unaccountably the signs are not transcribed, as in recent _CMS_ volumes, following the table in Olivier and Godart (_Corpus Hieroglyphicarum Inscriptionum Cretae_ [Paris 1996] 17).

Part 1 concludes with a small group of MM III–Late Minoan (LM) I cushions (nos. 177–85), including fine naturalistic studies such as the “wild goat at bay” and “bull at the trough.” New impressions and drawings now help reveal crucial details of technique and iconography. More or less contemporary are seals of the “Talismanic Style,” grouped together with the somewhat later (LM I–II) “Cut Style” at the beginning of part 2 (nos. 187–275). The distinction between the two styles is now well understood, and it is puzzling to read that the Cut Style birds with outstretched wings (nos. 271, 272) are either “Talismanic” or “Cut Style” (23). No “Cut Style features” are to be observed on the talismanic goat (no. 247); and to classify numbers 205 and 229 as “non-standard” is risky. One cannot help wondering if certain observations were embedded at an early stage in preparing the volume and not removed or modified in the final redaction. This may also account for some outdated terminology (e.g., “man,” “woman,” instead of the more neutral “male/female figure”) and descriptions that are decidedly cursory when judged by standards of recent _CMS_ volumes prepared wholly by the Marburg team.

Pride of place in part 2 goes to the famous gold rings with cult scenes (nos. 277–81). The lengthy bibliographies (one of the enormous strengths of this volume) attest to their importance in our discussions of Minoan religious iconography. While some may still harbor doubts as to the authenticity of the “Ring of Nestor” (no. 277), other suspect pieces (including no. 336) are now fully rehabilitated. Owing to a highly unfortunate slip, a photograph of the Nestor ring appears again on page 697, devoted to Evans’ replicas of the “Ring of Minos” housed in Oxford. The correct dimensions for number 278 are 2.1 cm length, 1.2 cm width.

The remaining seals (nos. 282–514) are datable to the Late Bronze Age and are broadly arranged by subject matter: human figures, alone or interacting with animals, _Mischwesen_, animal studies, and finally ornamental motifs. Noteworthy are seven made of lapis lacedaimonius, quarried only near Sparta. Most of the seals, such as number 298 depicting a “minotaur,” were probably Cretan-made, as rightly noted in the commentary (479; contradicting the inexplicable statement that it may be a mainland product [24]). Otherwise unparalleled is the use of a soft stone (serpentine) for another seal depicting a “minotaur” (no. 300). In fact, the collection contains relatively few soft-stone seals of LM I and LM II–III date, a reflection of Evans’ aesthetic judgement perhaps, not of original output. Of considerable interest are the six “Mainland Popular” seals evidently found on Crete (e.g., nos. 477, 478 [perhaps by the same hand]). Even in the Armenoi cemetery near Rethymnon, they are not especially well represented (pace 9), accounting for a mere eight–nine pieces of a total 170 seals. Among the Late Bronze Age ornamental seals are several of fluorite that are also probably mainland-made (nos. 494, 496, 497). But similar seals with distinctive Cretan designs from Armenoi have been identified as calcite, and this may also be true of number 493.

Any volume of this size is bound to have minor blemishes, but these are far outweighed by the sheer delight in finally having the rich Oxford collection fully and systematically documented. Deep gratitude is thus owed to the patient dedication of the volume editors and the _CMS_ team in Marburg. Yet the appearance of this volume also causes profound disquiet, for it is the last to appear under the aegis of the present _CMS_ project. At the end of 2011, the _CMS_ archive will be transferred to Heidelberg University, where it will serve as a major resource for glyptic research and teaching. But the backlog of seals not published in the _CMS_ series is considerable: (1) seals in non-Greek collections omitted in the original volumes or acquired since their publication; (2) pieces that entered the Herakleion Museum after 1960; (3) “new” seals discovered elsewhere in Greece since the last “collecting” trip in 1999. The task is daunting. To ensure that the new archive is not a dead archive, to ensure that well more than 1,000 seals as yet unrecorded in volumes of the _CMS_ do not become “lost souls,” the scholarly community must give its full support, both moral and financial, to the new project.

iv Introduction 

The discovery of the Minoan culture of Crete by Sir Arthur Evans in the late 19 th  century 

cemented him as a foundational figure within Bronze Age Aegean archaeology. Many of his 

ideas continue to lead discussions in Cretan archaeology, including his assessments of religiously 

significant locations, the creation of Minoan culture, and his ideas surrounding the development 

of written language (Hitchcock 2012, 195; Burns 2012, 292; Tomas 2012, 340). His frameworks 

for understanding various aspects of Minoan life and history are continuously referenced, 

primarily his chronology of Cretan history and the concept of a palace-based central 

administration, referred to as the palatial economy (Tomkins & Schoep 2012, 67; Schoep 2012, 

113). Due to his influence in the field, despite excavations of Bronze Age mainland Greek and 

Cycladic sites already being well underway prior to his discoveries, his name and research are 

found throughout Bronze Age Aegean archaeology. For scholars of the Mycenaeans, this 

involved establishing their pottery chronology through the structure of Evans’ tripartite 

organization of Minoan pottery (Rutter 2012, 415). 

In the Cyclades, Evans’ influence manifested largely in the understanding and analysis of 

frescoes, where his ideas have rooted themselves in the minds of modern researchers (Newman 

2017, 213). In particular, Evans’ identification of the lepidopterans on the “Ring of Nestor” and 

on other artifacts as butterflies, and, subsequently, every other depiction of the insects in Minoan 

art found more recently, has been continuously unchallenged. 1 His argument hinges on his 

entomologist colleague, Professor Poulton, identifying floating objects nearby the insects as 

chrysalises without the “slightest doubt,” and further identification of the butterflies as 

specifically Common White butterflies ( Pieris brassicae ; Fig. 2 ) (Evans 1925, 53). This

> used throughout this paper with chapter-specific distinctions of use made when necessary.

1identification then leads Evans to attribute religious significance to the appearance of these 

butterflies: the white butterflies represent the soul being weighed to determine possible 

reincarnation, an idea based on later religious practices found in Zoroastrianism and Classical 

Greek literature (61-62). Though he analyzes multiple examples of lepidopterans in Mycenaean 

and Minoan material culture to come to this conclusion, each is inspected separately from its 

external context within the assumption that the figure is the Common White butterfly. Evans 

gives some consideration to the potential of the insects being white moths rather than butterflies, 

but quickly dismisses this due to the chrysalis identification and butterfly-looking appearance of 

the insects on the ring (55). Evans’ assertion that the many examples of lepidopterans he 

analyzed were butterflies has led the modern scholar down a similar road, with the convention he 

established becoming a crutch used in research. However, new information from the West House 

at Akrotiri not available to Evans provides grounds for challenging his assumptions. 

The site of Akrotiri on Thera presents a unique case of lepidopterans in a wall-fresco, 

named the Flotilla fresco, preserved with the rest of the fresco context and the majority of the 

building. The available information provided by the site allows for an in-depth analysis of the 

fresco within its original context, allowing researchers to contextualize both the lepidopteran 

motif, the fresco as a whole, and the visual program’s place in the city. This other evidence 

comprehensively contextualizes the artist’s decision to add the lepidopteran motif while 

considering the possibility of the motif’s placement outside of interpretational convention. 

Within this paper, I will explore the case of this specific wall-fresco’s lepidopterans using a 

multidisciplinary approach that challenges Evans’ assertions and proposes that the true identity 

of the insects in the Flotilla Fresco is as moths, not butterflies. 

2The island of Thera (modern-day Santorini) is located at the southern tip of the Aegean 

Sea, being one of the closest Cycladic islands to Crete (Fig. 3). The island was continuously 

inhabited throughout the Bronze Age spanning from about 3000 BCE to the late 17 th  c. BCE 

during the Late Cycladic period (1725-1625 BCE), when a major volcanic eruption occurred 

(Doumas 1983, 27; Doumas 2012, 759). 2 As a volcanic island, many eruptions have taken place 

there, with the most famous being the Late Cycladic I eruption mentioned. This eruption, as 

theorized by Spyridon Marinatos, may have had direct influence on the fall of the Minoans’ 

prominence and later takeover by the Mycenaean culture of mainland Greece (Doumas 1983, 

15). The major Late Cycladic city of Akrotiri on Thera, first excavated by Marinatos, was buried 

by this eruption (Fig. 4). Akrotiri, being incredibly well-preserved by ash from the eruption, is 

sometimes referred to as the “Bronze Age Pompeii” because of its many similarities to the 

Vesuvius eruption, and provides invaluable information and context for the Bronze Age 

settlements in the region (12). 

The city was excavated between 1967 and 1976, revealing over 10,000 square meters of 

the site (Doumas 1983, 13, 45). Due to the excavated portions positioning themselves squarely 

within the city, and other excavated sections, like Ballos, located much further away, potentially 

being suburb regions, it is estimated that the total size of the settlement spanned somewhere 

around 200,000 meters (45). Of the main city, ten buildings have been excavated, including 

Buildings Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta, Xeste 1, 2, 3, and 4, the House of the Ladies, and the 

West House (30). Through the archaeological evidence provided by these buildings, a picture of 

Akrotiri as a major Middle and Late Bronze Age port city emerges. Architectural evidence dating

3to the Middle Cycladic  (ca. 2200-1700 BCE)  shows signs of destruction by earthquakes, with 

subsequent rebuilding in a larger and more luxurious manner during the Late Cycladic support 

the city’s wealthy stature as a trade hub (44). Imported Minoan pottery found in the West House, 

a Syrian amphora from Building Delta, and Egyptian ostrich-egg-and-faience rhytons also from 

Building Delta, among other examples, similarly inform us of the wealthy individuals that 

resided in the city (Marinatos 1974, 24; Doumas 1983, 119). 

In addition to the architectural and material evidence pointing to the city’s connectivity to 

the wider Aegean and Mediterranean, the high volume of well-preserved frescoes found at the 

site provide more context to the significant wealth of the city. Seven out of the ten buildings 

excavated have some kind of fresco visual program preserved, with each building containing 

multiple frescoes throughout the many rooms within. Fresco-painting technology is largely 

credited as arriving in Thera from Crete, with Theran frescoes sporting a similar color scheme of 

white, yellow, red, brown, blue, and black (Doumas 1983, 56). The imagery in these frescoes 

ranges from human to animal to landscape, and the style varies from life-sized to miniature, with 

the frescoes often taking up seemingly odd spaces on walls, doorways, and windows (73). 

Interpretation of this imagery largely stems from Evans’ initial interpretations of Minoan art, as 

Theran and Minoan art are closely linked stylistically; an example of this is the assumption that 

figures with red skin are male and those with white skin are female (56). Evans’ assumption that 

any lepidopterans in Aegean art represent butterflies has also been attributed to those insects 

present in the frescoes of Thera, primarily the Flotilla Fresco section of the Miniature Fresco 

program in the West House (Fig. 5). 

The Miniature Fresco program constitutes one of the primary sources for understanding 

Theran perspectives on the environment and maritime-based culture of the Aegean. It spans the 

4entire upper register of each wall (except for the west wall) of Room 5 within the West House, 

with the Flotilla Fresco residing on the south wall. Within this fresco, five “butterflies” reside, all 

resting in various positions on the ships within the flotilla, specifically ships 1 and 2 in the 

procession, with labels starting at the upper leftmost ship (Fig. 6-7). The reason for the presence 

of these insects has been deliberated very little throughout scholarship, with one of the more in-

depth analyses of the insects spanning only seven paragraphs in Lyvia Morgan’s 234-page book, 

The Miniature Wall-Paintings of Thera  (Morgan 1988, 132-134). The first suggestion that the 

motif could be intending to represent moths and not butterflies appears in Panagiotakopulu et al. 

(1997) in discussion of a calcified silk cocoon discovered during excavation, but originally 

misidentified as a clay cylinder (Panagiotakopulu et al. 1997, 420; Panagiotakopulu 1997, 591). 

The original assumption of the identification of a butterfly stems from a combination of reliance 

on pre-established conventions by Evans and isolated artistic analysis completed without 

consideration of external context, which necessitates reassessment through a different, un-

tethered approach. 

Methods, Objective, and Outline 

This paper utilizes a multidisciplinary, holistic approach in identifying and analyzing the 

available information surrounding the Flotilla Fresco and wider West House based on the 

theories of Ian Hodder and Erwin Panofsky. The former describes a process of understanding 

material objects through all of their available context referred to as contextual archaeology. This 

includes the object’s inherent function as it prescribes meaning, as well as the social and 

historical meaning applied culturally as understood through the application of similarities and 

differences in comparison to other material (Hodder 1987, 1). By comparing the Flotilla Fresco 

5lepidopterans to those found throughout the Aegean, the variation in representation and function 

of the moths can be used as a method of contextualizing the presence of the motif. Hodder 

further discusses instances where a material can have its meaning changed depending on the 

external context provided, which will be discussed in relation to this Aegean comparanda and 

how, despite many similarities, the moth identification applies specifically to the Flotilla Fresco 

and cannot be applied to all lepidopteran depictions (8). 

Hodder also describes a system in which the “structure” that a material is surrounded by 

provides a basis for comparison and derivation of meaning; this method will be applied in the 

assessment of the Flotilla Fresco juxtaposed against both the rest of the Miniature Fresco 

program in Room 5 and other frescoes present in the wider West House (Hodder 1987, 8). 

Constructing the “structure” around the Flotilla Fresco involves examining both the physical 

evidence correlated with the fresco, such as the fresco itself and the archaeological evidence 

present within Room 5, as well as tangential information related to the imagery and West House. 

This includes understanding the economy of the period, similar instances of the motif, and 

archaeological evidence provided by the wider structure. Both direct and indirect evidence must 

be considered to provide a full picture of the cultural setting in which the motif was created in. 

The second methodology I employ is based on Panofsky’s iconology and focuses on 

analysis of the moth motif. His iconology describes a three-part system that aids in completing a 

full analysis of art. The first two parts, analyzing the pure form of the piece and the secondary 

subject matter, are both applied to understand the style and purpose of the fresco as an artwork 

and as an installation within a structure (Panofsky 1939, 5-6). The third facet, which requires an 

understanding of the cultural experience of the time, place, and person, is largely unable to be 

utilized in analyzing this artwork due to the lack of information, but can be inferred based on 

6other contextual information (7). The use of cultural/historical intrinsic meaning assessed 

through the first two parts of Panofsky’s method allow the personal intrinsic meaning, typically 

found through the third part, to be determined to a degree. This iconology serves as a starting 

point to base any artistic analysis on, allowing space for pushing the theory further in places 

Panofsky did not, primarily in the assessment of the cultural/historical angle of the interpretation 

to allow insight into the personal angle. Despite being an older theory, similarly to Evans, it still 

provides a solid foundation to continue research forward. 

Panofsky’s iconology, in conjunction with Hodder’s contextual archaeology theory, 

establishes the basic issue with most analysis of Minoan art—the entirety of meaning cannot be 

ascertained without understanding the culturally inherited knowledge available to the artist at the 

time of creation (Panofsky 1939, 11; Hodder 1987, 7). As this cultural knowledge is unavailable 

to modern scholars, the gap must be filled through other facets of the analysis, a process which 

has not been consistently applied in research largely due to the reliance on initial claims like 

those made by Evans. Both Panofsky and Hodder make clear in their respective works that one 

cannot assume their assumptions are inherently correct, nor that the ideas present in the modern 

day are equal to those in antiquity and can be interchanged with no consequence (Panofsky 1939, 

9; Hodder 1987, 10). This paper will address both concerns by establishing the known cultural 

and economic climate in the region that provided the environment for the creation of the Flotilla 

Fresco. By providing all possible associations of the lepidopteran motif, the context and method 

of the fresco’s creation, and its position within the context of the West House, the gaps in 

knowledge can be assuaged until further evidence becomes available. 

For the sake of clarity, the use of palatial terminology will be used in reference to Cretan 

sites which are identified to have a large administrative, or “palatial,” structure through available 

7archaeological evidence. As Akrotiri is neither Cretan nor has an identified palatial structure, it 

will not be referred to as such (Doumas 1983, 124). For consistency, this paper will utilize the 

high/absolute chronology of the Bronze Age based on radiocarbon dating of the Thera eruption 

rather than the low/relative chronology framed largely by typological sequences (Manning 2012, 

13, 20). As this thesis concerns the primary archaeological site of Thera, basing dates within the 

framework reliant on the eruption that destroyed said site is appropriate. 

This paper aims to deconstruct the methods, created prior to the breadth of information 

available to scholars today, used to analyze and assume meaning in art. The over-reliance on 

precedent set by Evans when establishing the artistic conventions of Bronze Age artwork has 

delayed new perspectives in the field. The presence of butterflies in the Flotilla Fresco has never 

been deeply explored, nor given a meaningful discussion as to its purpose in a fresco where 

seemingly all aspects follow a certain theme. Recent research has started exploring Evans’ 

various assignments of purpose within Minoan artwork and challenging their binary nature, 

establishing a wider recognition of the need for this type of analysis to be done (Newman 2017, 

213). By formatting a similar discussion within the context of the Flotilla Fresco lepidopterans, 

the reservations of current research in regards to Theran art and the reality of the artistic choices 

made by the Theran artist can be illustrated. Further, the importance of connections between art 

and its cultural and physical context can be reinforced, reducing the idea that art is extraneous to 

the environment it resides within. 

This thesis examines the probability of a motif previously assumed to be a butterfly in 

reality representing a moth, re-imagining our understanding of the artistic language of the Late 

Bronze Age Aegean. A holistic perspective of the possible identity of this lepidopteran motif 

requires analysis of all related information and context available. By understanding the full 

8context of the fresco’s production, the use of motifs, and the relation to the wider structure and 

the people who lived and worked within it, one can then truly deconstruct the meaning of the 

lepidopteran motif. This provides the necessary information to propose a specific identity for the 

Flotilla Fresco insects should one fit within this wider context. 

In Chapter I, the current scholarship surrounding the Bronze Age luxury goods trade, the 

ecology of the Aegean, and the effects of Minoan cultural diffusion throughout the region will be 

assessed to provide the surrounding context needed to analyze the site of Akrotiri. Chapter II 

both explores the archaeological evidence present at the West House found alongside the Flotilla 

Fresco and dismantles the typical explanation for the identification of butterfly by analyzing the 

artistic context of the fresco’s location, creation, and stylistic characterization. The final section, 

Chapter III, focuses on lepidopteran imagery throughout the Aegean, providing a large set of 

comparanda to compare to the West House examples. This intends to both build the case for 

moving away from Evans’ assertions of butterflies and to provide reasoning for a potential 

cultural homogenizing of butterfly and moth characteristics within the visual language of Aegean 

art. This section will further analyze the connections between the textile industry, the sea, and 

moths to establish a case for wild-silk production in the region. 

9Chapter I 

Minoan Affluence in Luxury Trade and Influence on Thera/Wider Aegean 

When considering the Bronze Age Aegean, there are three main cultural groups. These 

are the Mycenaeans on mainland Greece, the Minoans on Crete, and the cultures of the Cyclades. 

During the period leading up to the Theran eruption in the late 17 th  century BCE, the dominant 

cultural group is the Minoan culture of Crete, who maintained widespread influence over the 

Aegean starting in the Middle Bronze Age ( 2000-1725 BCE)  before losing prominence in the 

Late Bronze Age, specifically towards the Late Minoan IIIA period ( 1425-1300 BCE)  (Niemeier 

1984, 207-8). As they resided on an island, the Minoans were a heavily maritime-based society. 

Original assertions by Sinclair Hood of the Minoan role in the Aegean is that of savage 

colonizers exerting their force and control over the neighboring Cycladic and mainland towns, 

though this image has been softened by more recent scholarship (Hood 1984, 33). Modern 

interpretations are much more neutral, assessing that the available evidence indicates a reciprocal 

relationship of some kind favoring the Minoans on Crete due to their evident prosperity (Nerling 

2014, 47). Minoan influence on the region is inseparable from any attempt at understanding the 

wide inter-connectivity of the Mediterranean and the economic relations present between various 

powers. 

Early Bronze Age trade was principally restricted to other Aegean sites in the Cyclades, 

along the mainland Greek coast, and in western Anatolia, largely aiding in the prosperity of the 

Cyclades due to their limited natural resources (Burns 2012, 293). Prepalatial Crete  (ca. 3100-

2100 BCE)  during this period was connected by trade to Egypt, as evidenced through changes in 

early Minoan pictorial art on seal stones (294). This trade continued into the Middle and Late 

10 Bronze Age (ca . 2000-1300 BCE) , when Crete was connected to Egypt and the Near East both 

through a direct southward sailing route and pre-established trade routes following the seasonal 

wind direction (Creisher 2015, 30). Other major contacts included Cyprus, the Hittites in 

Anatolia, Italy, and the city of Ugarit in modern-day Syria (Burns 2012, 297). All of these 

various connections to Mediterranean cultures resulted in an expansive trade network dominated 

by the Minoans during the height of their prominence in the Late Bronze Age. 

Trade in luxury goods was rampant in the Mediterranean during the entirety of the 

Bronze Age, with many coveted goods sourced from all around the region, from both coastal and 

inland origins. Minoan prominence within this trade started during the Middle Bronze Age with 

the establishment of palatial administration centers—a development accompanied by a large 

decrease in imported luxury goods, and an increase in high-value raw material imports as well as 

an increase in exported Minoan goods found throughout the Aegean (Burns 2012, 295). Egyptian 

tomb paintings like that of Rech-mi-Re, decorating the tombs of officials serving the Pharaohs 

Hatshepsut  (ruled ca. 1479-1458 BCE) , Thutmosis III  (ruled ca. 1479-1425 BCE) , and 

Amenhotep II  (ruled ca. 1427-1401 BCE) , depict Minoans specifically as bringers of luxury 

goods, emphasizing Crete’s leadership of the luxury goods market (Fig. 8) (Strøm 1984, 192). 

The importation of raw materials like metals and ivory to Crete demonstrates an emphasized 

switch from consuming luxury goods to producing them (296). The famed Uluburun shipwreck, 

carrying ten tons of copper ingots among many other high-demand raw materials, was sailing 

west towards the Aegean prior to its sinking, furthering this idea of importing raw materials to 

export processed goods (300). 

The main example of Crete’s exported luxury is Kamares ware pottery, a style of ceramic 

known for its elaborate decoration through various motifs and pigments and “eggshell thin” 

11 appearance created through a mastery of the kiln (Evely 2012, 394). The appearance of imported 

Kamares ware pottery in the Eastern Mediterranean during the LBA combined with the adoption 

of Minoan styles of living and/or technologies by Cycladic communities and the presence of 

Minoan communities as far as Miletus in Anatolia show an increase in cultural influence and 

prominence sometimes referred to as the “Minoanization” of the Aegean (Burns 2012, 295). This 

“Minoanization” is clearest in Akrotiri, where the adoption of Minoan culture was strongest and 

a similar level of wealth and prosperity was achieved prior to its destruction (Branigan 1984, 52). 

Along with Kamares ware, other ceramics, textiles, metalwork, and faience were also 

exported. Some examples of the latter two exports include gold foil beads, created through a 

mold technique and made in vast quantities, and faience inlays, which were frequently used in 

jewelry and other adornments alongside metalwork (Evely 2012, 392, 394). Textile exports 

appear in multiple ways. Fully produced cloth may have been exported from Crete as early as the 

pre-palatial Early Minoan period  (ca. 3100-2100 BCE) , but it was fully integrated by the Late 

Minoan (Burke 2012, 431). As the primary loom used in the Aegean at this time was the warp-

weighted loom, loom weights provide a large portion of the context surrounding textile 

production and Minoan influence on it (430). Though there are three main styles of loom weights 

found on Crete, those being the cuboid, melon, and discoid styles, the discoid style is particularly 

descriptive of the Minoans (Fig. 9) (433). Used from the Early Minoan II  (ca. 2650-2200 BCE) 

through the Late Minoan III  (ca. 1420-1050 BCE)  periods, the discoid loom weight has been 

found throughout the Aegean at many Cycladic sites, including Akrotiri, and were highly 

standardized to facilitate various intricate weaves and patterns (433). The Cycladic island of Kea, 

in particular, shows the gradual encroachment of Minoan influence through loom weight finds: 

Anatolian styles typical of a horizontal loom are the most common in the Middle Bronze Age 

12 (ca. 2100-1700 BCE) , but the discoid style becomes the dominant version by the Late Cycladic I 

(ca. 1700-1600 BCE)  (434). Akrotiri has unearthed the largest number of loom weights out of 

any Bronze Age Cycladic site, all of which are the Minoan discoid style (Tzachili 1990, 381). 

Another facet of the textile industry was the establishment of murex production sites and 

the export of Tyrian (or murex) purple dye. This dye is created using murex snail shells, a species 

of mollusk native to the Mediterranean, and requires immense labor to produce, setting the high 

cost for the pigment. As Middle Bronze Age Crete was likely the originator of production of the 

opulent purple dye, the spread of Minoan influence throughout the Aegean and wider 

Mediterranean directly caused the spread of this dye, cementing it as a status symbol (Kremer 

2017, 174). There are thirteen excavated Middle Minoan murex production sites present on Crete 

alone, which include the main palatial site of Knossos (176). Production sites in the Levant 

appear around the Late Minoan as well, with the region likely gaining the technology through 

interactions with Crete over hundreds of years (178). Murex purple remained culturally relevant 

all the way through the Medieval Roman period  (ca. 400-1400 CE) , well after the collapse of the 

Minoan culture, cementing Minoan cultural export status within the entire history of the ancient 

Mediterranean, not just the Bronze Age. 

Also among these luxury goods produced and diffused by the Minoan culture are wall 

frescoes , a type of  mural art used to decorate the interior walls of a variety of elite buildings and, 

occasionally, tombs (Immerwahr 1990, 11). This technology was adopted largely from Egyptian 

and Eastern Mediterranean influence during the Middle Bronze Age (Chapin 2014, 7). The two 

principal methods of fresco creation the Minoans used are  secco  and  fresco ; secco  describes the 

application of water-based pigment mixed with lime and then applied to a dry wall —a less stable 

method —while  fresco  is the application of water-based pigment to wet lime plaster, creating a 

13 chemical bond between the two and, therefore, a much hardier painting (Immerwahr 1990, 14). 

Minoan frescoes also maintain a standard, recognizable color palette of red, yellow, blue, and 

black sourced from a variety of mineral pigments. Variations of those colors resulted from 

mixing the pigments with other substances, whereas unpainted lime plaster made up any white 

coloring (15). Minoan cultural motifs seen in other luxury art-forms are prevalent in the 

surviving frescoes, including griffins, double axes, and bull-leapers. The primary locus of Cretan 

frescoes is Knossos, which has been touted as the center for Minoan fresco production and 

development as a cultural practice (Boulotis 1997, 845). 

Minoan fresco painters traveled around Crete and the wider Aegean performing art 

commissions for wealthy patrons, going as far as Egypt in some cases (Boulotis 1997, 845). 

Minoan-style frescoes discovered at Tell el-Dab’a, Egypt, in an early Eighteenth Dynasty  (ca. 

1550-1295 BCE)  palace, display both the  secco  and  fresco  techniques and the color palette of 

blue, red, black, and yellow, and depict common Minoan imagery of bull-leapers, griffins, and 

mazes, indicating they were painted by a Minoan or Minoan-trained artist (Seeber 1997, 95, 91). 

Painter workshops likely existed and employed both traveling and sedentary artists, as many 

frescoes have shown periodic retouching and others, primarily those in Akrotiri, show evidence 

of both skilled painters and less-skilled assistants working in tandem (Boulotis 1997, 851-52). 

These artists, through their diffusion throughout the Mediterranean, unintentionally created a 

region-wide painting schematic for the Aegean that dictated the themes and style of painting 

regarded as distinctly Minoan, despite its traversal through the region and indigenous influences 

(846-7). The presence of a Minoan-influenced Aegean artistic schema is most recognizable at 

Akrotiri with the site’s vast amount of fresco evidence. 

14 Minoan influence on Theran art is undeniable; the frescoes generally retain the typical 

color palette of red, yellow, and blue, they are produced with the same combination of  secco  and 

fresco  techniques, and many of the motifs are similar. 3 Within the painting schematic established 

by Minoan art, Theran art retains its unique identity, largely through its use of naturalism within 

artwork (Warren 1997, 365). This culturally-combined artwork established a close proximity to 

Cretan culture for the owner of the building the frescoes were painted in as well as prominence 

in Theran culture, establishing the owner’s status through the rich decoration (Boulotis 1997, 

849). The presence of fresco painters on Thera trained in the Minoan style, regular destructive 

events like earthquakes (leading up to the Late Cycladic eruption) requiring painting repairs, and 

the influence of native Theran culture on the artwork all indicate the possibility of a fresco 

workshop in the city where local artists would train and work out of, similar to those present on 

Crete (Televantou 1997, 831). Fresco painting as a permanent fixture in the town of Akrotiri 

affirms the vision of wealth and luxury portrayed by its remains, working in combination with its 

roots in Minoan culture to function as a luxury good within the Late Bronze Age economy. 

Allowing the production of luxury goods was the use of local and imported raw materials. 

Locally available materials covered both the daily needs of the people and certain facets of the 

luxury goods production on Crete. The fibers used in spinning thread and weaving fabric for 

non-luxury goods primarily came from sheep and flax, similar to the rest of the Mediterranean 

(Burke 2012, 436). In making luxury perfumes, many resources local to the island were used, 

such as coriander, rockrose, and camphor (Koh and Birney 2017, 24-5). Some pigments for 

fresco painting were also often sourced locally, with black coming from carbon, ochre being 

commonly available, and white coming from the lime used in plaster (Immerwahr 1990, 16).
