for feasting and perfume-making (Brandon 2025, 222, 224). 

Other food sources were similarly available locally. Plant-based food sources include 

fruits such as grapes, figs, and olives, legumes, cereals, and barley for bread (Livarda and 

Kotzamani 2020, 237). The Minoans did hunt, providing deer, boar, hare,  agrimi , badger, fox, 

and beech-marten. This was combined with the domestication of certain animals including goats, 

pigs, and sheep (Wilkens 2003, 86, 88). Cattle were also present, but more commonly used for 

labor rather than meat (Doumas 1983, 118). Other domesticated animals not used for eating were 

horses, donkeys, and dogs, the amount of each varying depending on location (Wilkens 2003, 

88). As an island culture, sea-life was quite important, with fish including but not limited to 

mackerel, bream, red mullet, and tuna, along with octopus and squid (Parks 2025, 17-18).  Snails 

were also common, with other sea creatures like urchins, limpets, and tritons acting as delicacies 

(Doumas 1983, 118). As these locally available resources were sufficient for the needs and daily 

lives of Cretan people, the focus of import trade was the raw materials needed for participation in 

the luxury goods market. The natural environment both sustained and supplemented the 

production of luxury goods, providing the stability allowing artisans to combine local and 

imported resources into something uniquely Minoan. 

16 As mentioned, imported metals were required for the many industries on Crete, including 

luxury metalworking and bronze tool production. Copper, tin, and silver were sourced primarily 

from Cyprus, the Levant, and the Laurion silver mines in Attica; gold is much more difficult to 

directly source, having the potential to have come from the wider coastal Mediterranean or as 

inland as central Romania (Burns 2012, 291; Evely 2012, 390; Laffineur 2012, 446-47). Other 

raw materials intended for luxury refinement were  lapis lazuli , sourced from Afghanistan, and 

amber from the Baltic (Burns 2012, 291). Ivory, imported from Egypt, has been discovered on 

Crete in both its raw and processed states at Kato Zakros, a palatial site on the island’s eastern 

coast (Burns 2012, 291; Platon 1971, 245). This support from the wider Mediterranean allowed 

Crete to maintain its status as a highly influential center for luxury goods production. 

The significant influence of Minoan culture throughout the Aegean, especially on its 

closest neighbor Thera, is directly related to the material culture discovered by archaeologists. 

Akrotiri’s wealth as a trading hub is directly tied to Minoan influence and cultural dominance 

over the region. The West House Miniature Fresco program, which depicts maritime themes and 

a strong association with wealth and status, is a direct consequence of this, as the combined 

luxury goods trade and growing status of proximity to Minoan culture lead Thera to becoming a 

juggernaut of trade, and subsequently provided the wealth necessary for the fresco to be created. 

The fresco is similarly inseparable from the wider Mediterranean influences present, including 

those from Egypt, Crete’s largest economic partner, due to the technology’s Egyptian origin. The 

Minoans’ place within this luxury economy further provides context for the suggestion of moths 

within the fresco rather than butterflies, as their use of the local and foreign ecology to produce 

goods establishes the means for further innovation within all goods, including the realm of 

textiles. 

17 Chapter II 

Archaeological and Art-Historical Context of the Flotilla Fresco 

The luxury economy present in the region at the time of the Flotilla Fresco’s creation 

provides the backing for the West House’s role within the town of Akrotiri. The relationship 

between the house and the fresco, found through exploring the physical evidence found 

alongisde the fresco in the house’s remains, helps to inform on the purpose of the lepidopteran 

motif and potential moth identity. Additionally, the artistic history of the region and its effect on 

the Flotilla Fresco must be assessed to fully encapsulate the culture and society that the 

lepidopteran motif existed in. This chapter will first cover the structure of the West House itself, 

the current understanding of who the owner was, and the archaeological evidence found within 

the house. An artistic analysis of the motif will then be presented within the context of the 

development of a native Theran art style influenced by the wider Mediterranean. The insects 

present in the Flotilla Fresco will be referred to as moths in the first segment, and 

interchangeably referred to as moths, insects, and lepidopterans in the second segment as needed. 

Archaeological and Contextual Evidence from the West House 

The West House is a standalone structure directly next to the Triangle Square in Sector 

Delta of the excavated sections of Akrotiri, Thera (Fig. 11). This sector is understood to be 

outside the city center, which was farther north and likely destroyed in the eruption  (Doumas 

1983, 50) . Its full use-case is unclear, as the location indicates a residential structure, but the 

layout and many material finds indicate a more public purpose (Morgan 1988, 3). The building 

has three floors, with the middle floor, accessible from the street, containing multiple rooms with 

18 fresco decoration. The fresco discussed in this case is the Miniature Fresco located in Room 5, 

specifically the Flotilla section of this program (Fig. 5). The Flotilla Fresco, located along the 

upper register of the  south wall , depicts a fleet of seven elaborately decorated ships moving 

throughout the Theran caldera before pulling into the minor port of Akrotiri at Ballos (Friedrich 

and Sorenson 2010, 251). Though the intended event being depicted is highly debated, the fresco 

itself portrays rich, natural life with deer, dolphins, lilies, reeds, and other sorts of flora and fauna 

amidst multiple large ships, people, and cuboid towns in a heavily maritime-themed scene. The 

fresco follows the typical Minoan red-blue-yellow color scheme established in Chapter I, over a 

white lime background, having many figures and scenes colored in an unrealistic but stylistically 

cohesive manner . This allows every figure to stand out individually whilst remaining within the 

wider context of the artwork. 

Joining the Flotilla Fresco in Room 5 are fragments from numerous additional frescoes 

such as a similarly sized naval fresco that lined the upper register of the  north side  of the room, a 

small river scene along the upper register of the  east wall , two large fisherman frescoes within 

the middle register (one on the  north wall , the other on the  west),  and imitation polychrome 

veined marbling painting the lower register (Fig. 12-15). The fragments of the naval fresco likely 

depict a conflict, as there are figures that appear to be bleeding out in the ocean and others 

wearing boar-tusk helmets and holding spears. The northwest fisherman, a boy with a blue 

shaved scalp, is holding three blue fish with white stomachs, and the northeast fisherman, also a 

boy with a blue shaved scalp, is holding seven fish in his right hand and five in his left, all of 

which are blue with yellow stomachs. Walking into the room from the northeast entryway, a 

person would have been greeted by the two fishermen, their eyes at about an average adult’s eye 

level, directing them to the north corner of the room. 

19 The West House as an archaeological site has provided ample evidence for both the 

owner being a prolific member of Theran society and the building itself—and by extension the 

owner—being involved in various textile-related activities. In Morgan (1988) and Barber’s 

(1987) assessments of Akrotiri, the evident prosperity of the area shown through the available art 

and architecture is regularly mentioned, along with the specific peculiarity of the West House as 

a substantial, standalone structure among rows of town homes and apartment-style dwellings 

(Morgan 1988, 1; Barber 1987, 203). The location of the frescoes within the architecture of the 

house and their relation to each other, especially in Room 5 which contains the Flotilla Fresco, 

will be a center-point of discussion. A notable departure from the typical Theran architectural 

design in Room 5 is the placement of the main doorway entering from Room 3, as it is located in 

the middle of the wall rather than at the end, creating an odd internal organization for the house 

structure as the floorplan works around this placement (Palyvou 2012, West House, Room 5). 

The frescoes then work with the mid-wall entrance to create a full visual experience; the 

fisherman frescoes direct the viewer’s gaze to the western corner, which then slides up to follow 

the upper frieze course through the Naval Battle and River Scene, leading the eye clockwise 

around the room, before ending with the Flotilla Fresco’s return to Akrotiri. The intentions of the 

artist in directing the gaze in this way portrays the Miniature Fresco as a narrative scene, placing 

the viewer in the context of the history presented before them, implicating the house’s owner 

requested these events be depicted this way. 

The artistic direction of the Miniature Fresco leads the viewer towards a specific 

understanding of the scenes depicted, interacting with them and their understood cultural context 

to portray its intended meaning.  As Lyvia Morgan, in her book  The Miniature Wall Paintings of 

Thera , states, “there can be little doubt that the decoration of [rooms 4 and 5] was pre-planned in 

20 its entirety and executed with each part in mind,” (Palyvou 2012, West House, Room 5; 155). 

The overall theme of the frescoes throughout the house is consistently nautical in nature, with 

Morgan arguing a maritime connection for the many motifs, animals, and human depictions 

throughout the building (Morgan 1988, 165). For example, the use of birds as prow decorations 

could stem from literal bird-shaped identifying implements, the possible use of birds as 

navigation aids, and/or as a symbolic guide on the prow to lead the ship in the correct direction 

(66-67). The “cat-chasing-waterfowl” motif seen in the River Scene fresco is connected through 

the food chain: the waterfowl lives off the sea, and the cat lives off the waterfowl, therefore also 

living off of the sea (43). This tangential connection is treated with a similar weight in her 

assessment of the cohesiveness of the theme within the fresco program. 

The identified butterflies, which are given an acknowledgment of symbolizing greater 

esteem, but otherwise dismissed as “encapsulating a sense of motion,” are not attributed a more 

direct connection to the nautical theme (Morgan 1988, 133).  As previously established, maritime 

activity carries with it connotations of the textile industry and the luxury industry provided by it. 

The connection between wild-silk production and maritime associations held by the textile 

industry is more tangential than direct, but, per the cat-chasing-waterfowl example, does not 

discredit it. Wild-silk is also a luxury good, requiring a large amount of labor to create similar to 

Murex dye, but butterflies, by contrast, do not have any associations with wealth or the textile 

industry (Panagiotakopulu 1997, 586). Modern examples of wild-silk hold similar connotations 

of wealth, such as that of silk produced by moths in the  Anaphe  genus used by the Yoruba of 

Nigeria to denote cultural purity and status (McKinney and Eicher 2009, 45). However, these 

associations do apply directly to the presence and identification of moths within the fresco as 

they represent another aspect of the textile industry already being recalled to the viewer. 

21 Butterflies would make little sense within this fresco program already identified as being very 

intentionally designed. 

Looking at the West House from a different angle, insights into the life and dealings of 

the owner of the house are prevalent. Early on, interpretations of the Flotilla Fresco included it 

being the final part of a larger story of an overseas military voyage ending in the ceremonial 

homecoming of the sailors (Doumas 1992, 47). This has led to many crediting the so-called 

captain of the flotilla as the owner of the West House himself, commissioning these paintings to 

express his status as the commander of the flagship vessel (ship 2) and a crucial aspect of the 

fresco’s later interpretations (Fig. 16) (Doumas 1983, 77, 106). As a wealthy Akrotirian, using 

these frescoes as a show of status was a given; it was likely considered a privilege to indulge and 

use art in this manner (Televantou 1997, 832). The earliest interpretation of the Flotilla Fresco by 

original excavator Spyridon Marinatos similarly claims the person seated within the cabin of 

Ship 2 must have been the “admiral” of the fleet, and, thus, also the owner of the West House 

(Marinatos 1974, 43). Regardless of the owner’s specific role in the miniature frieze course, his 

potential presence within the paintings signifies his high status within Theran society through his 

participation in this venture (Doumas 1992, 49).  If the owner is indeed the “admiral” seated in 

the cabin of the flagship, then the use of lepidopterans as decoration for the ship becomes key in 

understanding the message portrayed by the fresco. 

Modern interpretations of the figure follow the same general trend of viewing the owner 

as involved in the depicted scenes, but include the archaeological finds of the house to support 

new conclusions—primarily, the understanding of him as a major trader within the textile 

industry of Thera and the wider Aegean. Hitchcock (2016) describes the multiple instances 

within the house of possible depictions of various fiber types including cotton, flax, sea-silk, and 

22 wool in the frescoes or their implied existence through material finds like large bathtub 

fragments for washing fibers (28, 29). An assessment of the “star” motif that accompanies the 

moths on the prows of both Ships 1 and 2, as well as appearing on other ship prows both alone 

and alongside other decorations, as cotton flowers is frequently cited as further evidence of the 

house’s, and therefore owner’s, connection to textiles (Panagiotakopulu 1997, 588). Additional 

evidence of lavish feasting is found throughout the West House in the ceramic finds. These 

included a large volume of lavish conical cups and pouring/libation vessels found in Room 5, 

which fits the owner’s status as a wealthy Akrotirian well-known within both public and market 

spheres of influence (Hitchcock 2016, 29). As  the maritime theme of these frescoes is likely 

descriptive of the owner of the West House and displays their prominence in Akrotiri society, this 

emphasis of textile-related motifs throughout both the Flotilla Fresco and others within the house 

must also be descriptive of the West House owner. The concepts of wealth alluded to by the 

presence of these frescoes, and the multiple material finds like high-end pottery, further illustrate 

the character of the owner and house, and is only bolstered by the material evidence found at the 

site. 

The archaeological evidence within both Room 5 and the wider West House pursues an 

idea of wealth and luxury combined with strong ties to the Akrotiri textile trade. Within Room 5 

itself, aside from the many elaborate frescoes already described in-depth, various fragments of 

imported Minoan vases were found mixed in with the fragments of the Flotilla Fresco, along 

with other more general pottery wares likely stored in the cabinets that lined the walls of the 

room (Marinatos 1974, 24-25). Further evidence of luxury comes from Room 4, where frescoes 

of  ikria  lined every wall in the room (including the subdividing walls), and Room 4 α had an 

elaborately decorated window with painted marbling on the sill and marbled vases along the 

23 sides with red lilies coming out, along with a vessel described as a “ pyxis -strainer” (Fig. 17) (25). 

The  ikria  of Room 4 are the same structure as the “cabins” present on the ships in Room 5, but 

are depicted much larger and in greater detail—the term  ikria  having been co-opted by S. 

Marinatos from its original scaffolding connotation to be used in this context to mean ship cabin 

(Shaw 1990, 167). The Priestess Fresco, located in the doorway connecting rooms 4 and 5, also 

presents this luxurious nature of the house through her elaborate clothing and potential link to 

sea-silk, along with the find of a locally made, highly decorated polychrome  kymbai  (a uniquely 

Theran style of elongated, oval high-walled plate with handles) in an unspecified location of the 

house (Fig. 18) (33-34;  National Archaeological Museum 2024 ). 

The primary object with potential textile connections in the West House is a large tub, 

initially assumed to be a bathtub, residing in a sub-division of Room 4 (Marinatos 1974, 28). As 

the functional purpose of the West House is unclear as to whether it had a domestic, economic, or 

mixed use, there is the potential for the tub to be used for other activities like washing or dyeing 

fabric rather than human hygiene. In the processing of silk, the cocoons must be boiled, 

degumming the fibers into a workable state, providing another potential use for this tub 

(McKinney and Eicher 2009, 53). Additionally, over 450 flat discoid loom weights were found in 

Room 3, which connects directly to Room 5 and the rest of the house. At Akrotiri, over 950 loom 

weights have been excavated, all within a weight range of 125-285 grams, establishing the 

potential for many different sizes and fineness of thread being produced (Tzachili 1990, 381). 

Out of the ten buildings excavated at Akrotiri, only four contained loom weights (the others 

being Buildings Alpha, Beta, and Delta), further establishing the West House as uniquely well-

situated for textile production (Hitchcock 2016, 21).  The space in Room 3 was large enough to 

employ 4 or 5 warp-weighted looms, each needing roughly 20-30 loom weights. The number 

24 found within the space far exceeds this minimum requirement, indicating that these extra weights 

were likely used for different types and sizes of yarn and various weave patterns and techniques 

(Tzachili 1990, 385-86). 

There is a notable lack of spindle whorls found at the site, though this can be interpreted 

as evidence of trade of raw and processed materials due to the lack of geologic and 

environmental infrastructure present at Akrotiri not allowing for large-scale processing of wool 

and flax (386). The likelihood of Room 3 being some form of textile manufacturing space is 

highly probable. The additional evidence for the production of luxury goods in the neighboring 

rooms further illustrates a picture of the West House being owned by a wealthy individual 

actively involved in the textile trade, drawing further conclusions that said textile trade was the 

primary source of their wealth. This explains the presence of moths within the Flotilla Fresco, 

then, as both literal and symbolic representations of said wealth tied to the textile industry. 

Art-Historical Analysis of the Flotilla Fresco 

The styling of Minoan and Minoan-influenced frescoes can be used to evaluate various 

elements and overall narratives presented through the medium. Minoan fresco painting, as an 

industry, was heavily influenced by Egypt’s artistic canon, both in figure and color, starting in the 

Middle Bronze Age due to deep trade connections (Chapin 2014, 4, 12). Minoan-style frescoes 

found at Tell el’Daba dating to the 18 th  Dynasty, demonstrating the reality of Minoan artists 

being commissioned outside of the Aegean, exemplifies the widespread cultural influence and 

exchange between Crete and the wider Mediterranean (27). The famous Ayia Triada Sarcophagus 

(LM IIIA, ca. 1420-1330 BCE) mirrors many traits found in 18 th  Dynasty carved sarcophagi 

meant for noble families in Egypt, being both chest-shaped and made of stone (Fig. 19) (38). The 

25 artwork decorating the sarcophagus exhibits influences from Mycenae, Crete, and Egypt, 

displaying Minoan-styled clothing and double axes, bull sacrifice common in Mycenaean 

paintings, and funerary practices indicative of an Egyptian origin (39). Though from a later 

period than the frescoes at Akrotiri, the sarcophagus presents the culmination of the strong inter-

connectivity of the arts in the Mediterranean prior to the collapse of the Bronze Age. 

Akrotiri is especially lucrative in displaying Egyptian and Minoan artistic influences. The 

blue monkeys present in many Theran frescoes, like those in House Beta, depict a species of 

monkey, the vervet, native to Nubia and are emblematic of the deep connection between Egypt, 

Crete, and Thera and the continuous impact Egyptian art had on Minoan and Minoan-influenced 

stylings (Fig. 20) (Presiosi and Hitchcock 1999, 128). Within the West House, the Fisherman 

Fresco on the north wall accompanying the Flotilla Fresco in Room 5 similarly shows this 

blending of Egyptian and Minoan influences in Theran art. The positioning of the boy’s 

shoulders as frontal and the hips as profile to show a composite perspective of the human figure 

demonstrates Minoan and Near East/Egyptian conventions working in tandem (Chapin 2014, 

22). Similarly, Marinatos described the fish being held as depicting “the usual hybrid nature of 

Minoan flora and fauna,” when observing the freshly excavated frescoes (Marinatos 1974, 36). 

Architecture was affected by these influences as well, with many buildings in Akrotiri featuring 

Minoan architectural stylings and some being entirely Minoan in construction; some buildings at 

the site of Ayia Irini similarly display this phenomenon (Presiosi and Hitchcock 1999, 135; 

Roche 2026, 11). The import of Minoan weavers and weaving techniques to Thera was also 

established in the previous chapter, displaying further the cultural diffusion occurring in the 

Aegean during the Late Bronze Age. The frequent use of Minoan culture, largely influenced by 

Egyptian culture, by elites in Akrotiri to represent themselves indicates a strong association 

26 between Cretan culture and high status, fitting with the assessment of the West House owner as 

an elite intending to show off their status through the artwork within the building (Roche 2026, 

12). 

Despite the large influence that Minoan art and culture had on the elite in Akrotiri, Theran 

artwork still retains a clearly Theran style utilized expertly by local artists. A common trait of 

these frescoes is their use of blank space to embody a free and spacious composition. Fritz 

Blakolmer, in his analysis of Theran, Mycenean, and Minoan styles, interprets this use of blank 

space as representing a “provincial” version of Minoan art; the lack of filled space would have 

appeared “unfinished” to the Minoan eye and indicates that this aspect of Theran art surely 

proved it was simply an unskilled copy of Minoan conventions with little Cycladic influence 

(Blakomer 2016, Akrotiri). Other scholars such as Colin Renfrew give the style more credence, 

viewing the use as impressing a sense of openness and a brightness upon the viewer not seen in 

traditional Minoan works (Renfrew 1997, 152). The use of white as the background for many of 

the frescoes present at Akrotiri —a feat requiring skilled painters due to the small margin of error 

—as well as the use of an expanded color palette based on a Minoan one displays the 

intentionality Theran artists had when creating these artworks and the manipulation of Minoan 

conventions to create a hybrid Minoan/Theran style (Televantou 1997, 837). Christina 

Televantou’s research has asserted that this uniquely Theran fresco style stems from the existence 

of a painting workshop in the city, so that the art form developed within the previous Cycladic 

context alongside Minoan influences rather than Minoan influence completely supplanting any 

native Theran artistic stylings (Televantou 1997, 831). Though the frescoes of Akrotiri have been 

frequently cited as the clearest example of “Minoanization” in the Aegean, they still maintain a 

27 sense of originality, and can not be assumed to be simply Minoan copies that follow all of the 

same artistic conventions  (Presiosi and Hitchcock 1999, 124). 

Theran art, as previously established, follows a mixture of native and Minoan practices, 

with Egypt’s influence ever present as well. Christina Televantou’s categorization of the artistic 

styles of Thera aids in understanding the breadth of artistic liberty present at Akrotiri. She asserts 

the existence of three primary painting styles present at Akrotiri: 1) the “Minoanizing” style that 

more strictly follows the Minoan canon, 2) the “formal-abstract” style, which focuses on abstract 

renderings within a formalized order-of-operations, and 3) the “free” style, where the artist 

utilizes their understanding of the Minoan canon to “play around,” freely creating compositions 

without restriction (Televantou 1997, 838-40). No fresco fits solely into one of these categories, 

rather being composed of a mixture of each to varying degrees. The Miniature Fresco of the West 

House primarily follows the first of these styles, generally following a Minoan canon for its 

design. This is largely evident through the uniformity of the people and smaller details like 

animal feet and the consistency in style and coloration of the entire fresco program, though 

Televantou observes that the artist has a tendency towards naturalism in their work (838). She 

describes the originality of the artist, where they break away from the Minoanizing style into a 

more free form one, as revealed through the “harmonious repetition of motifs” and various 

unique uses of the available space for a cohesive atmosphere and presentation (838-39). The 

artist’s use of Minoan techniques and themes combines with the limitations of space and the 

intended message of the artwork to create a work inseparable from its Theran origin. 

Theran use of of naturalism appears to denote the cultural importance of a motif due to its 

frequent use with known culturally important motifs, such as the crocus (Warren 1997, 371). 

Naturalism within Theran and Minoan art is utilized thoroughly when depicting various flora and 

28 fauna, and has been observed by Christina Televantou as a specific quirk of the Miniature 

Fresco’s artist. In contrast to naturalism is essentialism, which entails is depicting something 

with the essential characteristics but not recognizably as any specific motif (Warren 1997, 365). 

The extent of naturalism is not evenly distributed across all motifs; motifs exist within a sliding 

scale between true naturalism and true essentialism, where the viewer must incorporate their 

cultural knowledge to identify the degree of naturalism/essentialism present in any given image 

(Warren 1997, 365). The clearest example of naturalism in Theran frescoes are the crocus and 

lily, with which Theran art depicts the flowers accurately enough for academics to identify the 

specific genus being depicted for both plants (fig. 21-22). The artists accurately but stylistically 

rendered the leaf number, shape and size, petal shape and size, and bloom clustering of both 

flowers and the characteristic red styles of the crocus (371, 373). 

Despite this, there is still clear artistic liberty taken in depicting these flowers. The crocus 

petals are shown in a wide variety of colors and shades extending past their natural range, 

including red, pink, blue, white, purple, and yellow, but none with the distinctive petal veining of 

the crocus (Warren 1997,  371). Lilies are generally more accurate color-wise, but have other 

changes made to them through the hybridizing of different species of lily into one depiction 

(373). The structure of lilies is also sometimes changed by adding an extra seventh petal and 

stamen to provide visual harmony within the two-dimensional representation (Baumann 2006, 

392). Later Mycenaean examples of lilies depict them with the six petals and stamens as in 

nature, marking this change as a primarily Theran style (394). These stylizations are not the same 

as an essentialistic representation, and should not be confused. Peter Warren (1997) argues that 

Theran depictions of reeds and papyrus fall into this essentialist designation. The reeds 

referenced occur in Xeste 3 and, rather than having naturalistic grouping or accuracy in the 

29 depiction, are shown with straightforward shapes and in a golden color, presenting the essence of 

reeds and allowing them to naturally frame the (naturalistic) bird surrounded by them (Fig. 23) 

(378). The papyrus similarly shows the essential features of the papyrus plant: leaves sourced 

from the base, a long and plain stem, and a flared, fan-shaped head vaguely reminiscent of the 

plant’s natural presentation (Fig. 24) (378). In these cases, the essentialism of the motif reduces it 

to set-dressing, establishing these depictions as separate from the stylization found on 

naturalistically depicted motifs meant to stand out within these frescoes. The combination of 

artistic liberty and naturalism in the depiction of focal floral and faunal motifs will be referred to 

as “stylized naturalism” for the remainder of this paper in analyzing the moth motif. 

Within this concept of stylized naturalism, the stylization of motifs juxtaposes their 

naturalistic character by impressing a culturally charged perspective onto the viewer. Depictions 

of flora and fauna that contain some semblance of cultural importance or status are created using 

a combination of naturalism and artistic liberty. The need for naturalistic forms is to assert a 

recognizable base for the animal or plant in question so there is no confusion about what is being 

shown. The  agrimi , an animal frequently depicted throughout the Aegean, is consistently 

depicted with a naturalized form that is both distinct and anonymous; it is unquestionably an 

agrimi , but no specific individual is shown, allowing for the cultural associations of the motif to 

take precedence over other relations (Fig. 25) (Polinsky 2018, 56). The situation is the same for 

the crocuses and lilies, with the aforementioned artistic changes rooted in a need for visual 

cohesion, preserving their essence and cultural meaning. Many of these changes can also be 

traced back to inherent limitations of the artistic style. The primary use of profile to depict 

motifs, as influenced by Egyptian and subsequently Minoan artistic conventions, limits the range 

of options available to the artist. In the case of the seven-petaled lilies, this limitation likely led 

30 to the addition of the extra petal and stamen, as the visual symmetry sought by the artist was 

unable to be achieved otherwise. Theran artists have proven themselves to be experimenters in 

the medium, shown by the composite positioning of the Fisherman Frescoes in the West House 

being a combination of multiple influences, but these limitations can not be ignored when 

analyzing their use of motifs. Thus this idea of stylized naturalism is composed of three factors 

working in tandem to varying degrees: the literal depiction of the motif, the limitations of said 

depiction, and the meaning intended by the motif’s inclusion. 

The many motifs present in the Flotilla Fresco of the West House are emblematic of this 

stylized naturalism. The bird decorating the prow of Ship 4 has a clear silhouette, yellow color, 

and some lined detailing. It shows a natural form that clearly expresses the intended subject 

while still maintaining stylization through the unnatural color choice, and its meaning, which has 

already been explained in the West House section of this chapter, is consistent with the rest of the 

fresco. The many dolphins in the scene follow suit; they are clearly identifiable as dolphins with 

a thin snout, curved teardrop body, and fins in the right places, while being shown with 

multicolored oscillating stripes based on the model species’ band of pigmentation running along 

the side (Fig. 26) (Morgan 1988, 61). Their indication of the scene’s sea-based location and 

implication of swift movements are clearly conveyed as well (133). These motifs are not 

obviously inhibited by the functional limitations of the medium and can thus be determined to 

follow the tenets of stylized naturalism. In applying this analysis to the moth motif, more 

considerations need to be made to address the full extent of each factor of stylized naturalism to 

truly assess the identity of these figures as moths. 

31 Stylized Naturalism within the Flotilla Fresco Moths 

In addressing the literal depiction of the motif, the reasons for the assumed butterfly label 

must be discussed. The features commonly used to argue for butterflies include the color, shape, 

and positioning of the wings and the shape of both the antennae and body. The yellow color seen 

on all five moths on the ships is easily comparable to the use of color for crocuses; assuming the 

intended moth was  Saturnia pyri  or  Pachypasa otis , the use of yellow to stand in for the brown 

wings of the moths is a lateral move, as it lightens the color without changing the hue too 

drastically. The use of one of the other palette colors, such as red or blue, would have contrasted 

much more clearly against the white background of the fresco, indicating that using yellow was 

an intentional choice. Additionally, the “eyes” depicted on the wings of all five moths reflect 

those present on the wings of  Saturnia pyri , with a matching dark outline, lighter “sclera,” and 

dark “pupil.” As other lepidopteran examples, explored in chapter III, have depicted the “eyes” 

differently to be just circles or a single ring, this alignment with the natural reality is notable. 

Another facet is the use of scale in the fresco. Though the fresco is painted in a miniature style, 

and is thus already working on an unrealistic scale, the moths are depicted nearly equal in scale 

to the surrounding dolphins and other bowsprits. The notably large size of the  Saturnia pyri  moth 

immediately comes to mind as factoring into the scale of the moth motifs. The use of key 

identifiable features from  Saturnia pyri  and  Pachypasa otis  in the motif serves as grounds for 

alignment of the motif with moths over butterflies. 

Despite the logical positioning presented by the first two features discussed, there is valid 

reasoning for the assumption that these motifs are butterflies primarily based on the shape of the 

body and antennae, and the positioning of the wings. When viewing the moths, the curled 

antennae, long body, and profile-wing view all immediately read to a modern audience as 

32 butterfly instead of moth. The first clue to why this brief observation is not entirely accurate is 

the previously established canon of naturalism allowing for a clear identification. The insects 

depicted do not clearly depict a specific genus of butterfly or moth, rather presenting an 

ambiguously “lepidopteran” visage. There is a decent likelihood that the artist was rendering 

these figures by synthesizing various lepidopteran elements, which would explain the eyes and 

color of  Saturnia pyri  and, in the case of the two on the prow of Ship 2, the spiked wings of 

Polygonia egea  (Coutsis 1997, 580). This choice indicates a cultural synthesis of lepidopteran 

features within the visual language, which is assessed more thoroughly in chapter III. 

Further support for this synthesis, or at least the effects of it on later periods, is the 

specific language used when referring to butterflies and moths within Attic Greek. As the initial 

assumption of every Aegean lepidopteran motif defaulting to “butterfly” originates from Evans, 

his use of the Attic Greek vocabulary surrounding said insect is valuable to mention. He defends 

his identification partly with the correlation between white butterflies and the word  ψυχή, 

meaning soul or spirit, with butterflies embodying the concept of a departed spirit (Evans 1925, 

54). He briefly entertains the idea that this word could also be referencing white moths, but 

dismisses this idea due to representations of butterfly chrysalises in Mycenaean art (55). The use 

of the term  ψυχή  to mean lepidopteran appears in three texts: Aristotle’s  History of Animals ,

Plutarch’s  Quaestiones Convivales , and Theophrastus’  Enquiry into Plants . Aristotle’s use of the 

word is indirect and reliant on the translation, as there are no key words to implicate a moth or a 

butterfly specifically, simply the context that whichever it is is the kind to not produce larvae 

(Arist., HA, 551a14). Plutarch, when describing the conundrum of “the chicken or the egg,” 

refers to a “winged animal” named  ψυχή  emerging from a dry shell, but gives no other details, 

leaving room for this to reference either moths or butterflies (Plu., Qconv., 2.636c). 

33 Theophrastus’s reference is the clearest, with the word translating to “insect,” but the direct use 

of “chrysalis” indicating a butterfly (Thphr., HP, 2.4.4). 

The Liddel, Scott, and Jones entry for the word is similarly impartial, describing it as 

meaning “butterfly or moth” (s.v. “ψυχή (n.).”). One other word,  φάλαιναν , can similarly refer to 

both butterflies and moths on an either/or basis ( LSJ , s.v. “φάλαιναν (n.).") . Moths and butterflies 

being referred to with the same language also appears in some modern languages like French, 

which refers to both insects with the same word,  papillion , with the simple addition of “of night” 

for moths (NCMNS 2021). This impartiality of language challenges Evans’ assumptions and thus 

leaves room for further investigation. The presence of moths and butterflies in Linear A is not 

known, and no characters in the script depict any similar-looking insects. The same goes for 

Linear B, which has no words known to translate to “butterfly” or “moth,” but the character “  𐀔 ,” 

read as “ma,” does vaguely resemble the insects. 

Additionally, only words that describe solely moths occur in Attic Greek. These include 

βρωστήρ/βρωτήρ, ἡπίολος, and σής all meaning “moth” and πυραύστης meaning “moth that gets 

singed in the candle”  (LSJ , s.v. “βρωστήρ/βρωτήρ (n.)," “ἡπίολος (n.)," “πυραύστης (n.)," “σής 

(n.),") . This later syncretism of lepidopterans in the Greek language is possibly residual from this 

Bronze Age synthesis of the two insects. The additional large showing of words solely referring 

to moths may also indicate a residual association of moths as somewhat culturally meaningful, 

which follows the understanding of moths as culturally important in the Bronze Age Aegean due 

to their textile and wealth associations.  The s ynthesis of the visual language of lepidopterans into 

an amalgamation of various characteristics then problematizes the use of the literal depiction of 

these motifs within the Flotilla Fresco to ascertain their true identity unlike with the other motifs 

present.  Therefore, the other factors of stylized naturalism, the limitations of the depiction and 

34 the intended meaning of the depiction, are taken into larger account than the literal depiction due 

to its unclear nature. 

The limitations imposed on the artist creating the Flotilla Fresco largely stem from two 

factors: the profile view limiting the possible positioning of elements and the size and location of 

the fresco. The positioning of the wings in profile has been a mainstay argument for why the 

lepidopterans present are butterflies rather than moths, as when at rest, in reality, butterflies 

generally hold their wings vertically over their back while most moths hold theirs horizontally or 

spread flat (NCMNS 2021). This argument is based on the assumption that the motif is a one-to-

one recreation of the natural reality of a butterfly unaffected by the medium within which it is 

presented. Per this research, the wing positioning can be explained by the style limitations of the 

fresco. As the entirety of the fresco exists within a profile view, the illustration of the wings in 

this same manner cannot be immediately assumed to be part of the literal representation of the 

insect. Understanding the Egyptian and Minoan influences on the Theran style, as previously 

established, informs that the profile view is the convention of the painting and not purely the 

artist’s decision. It cannot be considered a parallel to the hybrid composite view present in the 

Fishermen Frescoes, as they are inherently different artistic presentations. Thus the profile 

positioning of the wings of the lepidopteran is caused by the limitations of composition and 

convention rather than being a fully independent artistic choice. An additional consideration is 

that, if the artist had illustrated a realistic moth’s wing position, it would interrupt the movement 

of the figures in the fresco. If the moth had been positioned frontally, it would break the flow and 

precedent set by every traveling motif within the fresco. The moth, being a traveling motif itself, 

must move with the rest of the fresco and cannot be stationary, thus the profile view of the insect 

is not reason enough to disqualify its identity as a moth. 

35 Additionally, the size and location of the fresco itself must be taken into consideration. As 

it was placed along the upper edge of the wall against the ceiling, it would not have been close to 

the viewer, necessitating changes to maintain clarity and comprehension of the composition due 

to its miniature styling. The other facets of the insect used to declare it a butterfly include the 

antennae and the long body, both of which can be explained by these limitations. The size 

limitation is demonstrated fully by the presence of  ikria  both on the ships in the Flotilla Fresco 

and the much larger version in Room 4 of the West House. The  ikria  present on the ships display 

key features and decorations, including the garlands connecting the three posts at the top, the 

segmentation of the body, and the colorful painting decorating the exterior. The  ikria  of Room 4 

are able to show all of these in greater detail, with garlands of flowers, waves decorating the 

trimming, and the full painted exterior. They are also able to show details absent from the Flotilla 

Fresco; the lily-shaped decorations topping the three posts and different kinds of garlands made 

of beads with hanging flowers are not present in the miniature  ikria . The miniature ikria were 

changed to fit the miniature style of the fresco without losing their recognizability. The same can 

be said for the elongated body and large, curled antennae of the moths; they both create clear 

shapes recognizable as parts of the insect from far away while also displaying the direction of 

motion present in the fresco and preserving the visual cohesion of the painting. Thus the absence 

or simplification of details for the sake of clarity within the Flotilla Fresco cannot be used to 

deny the identity of the moths present. 

The intended meaning of the motif must also be considered. It has already been 

thoroughly established that the use of motifs is closely connected to their cultural significance 

and meaning within the fresco composition. Therefore the use of lepidopterans must also hold 

cultural weight, as does every other motif within the Flotilla Fresco. When comparing the 

36 cultural relevance of butterflies and moths to both the other motifs of the fresco and the 

surrounding evidence from the West House, moths clearly hold a stronger claim as the 

lepidopterans’ identity. To demonstrate this, the cultural associations of both insects will be 

assessed. 

Starting with butterflies, their main relevance comes from religion. Due to the assumed 

importance of the cyclical nature of life and the concept of regeneration, the butterfly, along with 

many other motifs like the octopus, squid, and mollusk, are assumed to be religious symbols due 

to their observable traits and life-cycle (Marinatos 1993, 196). This assumption heavily relies on 

the identification them as butterflies, despite the idea of regeneration through a chrysalis/cocoon 

also applying to moths. The use of octopuses, squid, and mollusks to display the idea of 

regeneration does relate the butterfly motif to the symbolic function of the sea, but the 

connection here is slight (195). Another potential relation between butterflies and the sea is the 

insects landing on ships to rest while migrating over open water, providing reason for the animal 

to be depicted as a bowsprit (Coutsis 1997, 582). This latter relation is much more tangible and 

holds slightly more weight than the religious connection. 

These connections to the sea fit within the maritime theme of the fresco, but not within 

the status nor textile implications that are also being impressed by the fresco. Butterflies having 

these ties to the sea does relate them indirectly to the textile industry, which has been previously 

stated as inextricably tied to the sea and its resources, but provides no true sense of status unless 

the West House owner was intending to impart a religious authority (which has not been 

observed in any analysis of the Flotilla Fresco). Any status association with butterflies, outside of 

their religious connotations, largely comes from their presence within the archaeological 

evidence as decorating signet rings and seal stones or being made out of luxury materials, 

37 examples of which are described in the next chapter. The luxury in these cases is sourced in their 

physical material, not the symbol itself, and is insufficient in describing the status of the West 

House’s owner as per the framing of the Flotilla Fresco. 

Moths, on the other hand, directly relate to the sea, the textile industry, and high status as 

the fresco and house suggest. As the source of raw silk to produce wild-silk, the connection to 

the textile industry is undeniable. The textile industry on its own has also already been suitably 

related to the sea and maritime activity due to the nature of Akrotiri and the wider Aegean being 

maritime societies. Murex purple and sea-silk, as previously explained, are sourced from the sea 

as they come from mollusks, and their required labor and scarcity, along with records throughout 

history describing these goods, indicates that they were incredibly luxurious goods. Wild-silk, 

which would have been sourced from moths, would have required a similar level of intense labor 

to process into silk, placing it on a similar level to Murex purple and sea-silk and therefore 

assigning a similar price and luxury (Panagiotakopulu 1997, 586). Panagiotakopulu (1997) also 

suggests that the cocoons were imported to Akrotiri for processing due to the lack of evidence 

and resources for the raising of moths (588). These factors very strongly relate moths to a 

cultural association with the sea, textile industry, and luxury, suitably describing the owner’s 

status through their positioning on the flagship and Ship 1. Thus the identity of moth satisfies the 

criteria to be a culturally meaningful motif per its utilization within the Flotilla Fresco, where the 

identity of butterfly does not. This means that the moth motif, though troubled in its literal 

depiction, follows the framework of stylized naturalism both in its execution and meaning. 

Therefore, it is reasonably sound to identify the insect as a moth based on its artistic merit. 

38 Chapter III 

Lepidoptera Depictions in Minoan Art and Their Relation to the Textile Industry 

Moths, as an important symbol of Minoan and Minoan-influenced Aegean cultures, are 

indirectly implicated through multiple sources. Along with their direct representation through art 

and imagery, moths indicate the possibility of a wild-silk industry in the Aegean, based on 

newfound archaeological evidence. To establish this, pictorial representations of lepidoptera, and 

similar symbology, will be described in detail to assess the volume and context of lepidopteran 

depictions. This is followed by contextual evidence implied through cultural associations to 

assess the plausibility of a wild-silk industry. The objective for this chapter is to make the case 

that specific instances of “butterflies” identified within the Flotilla Fresco of the West House in 

Akrotiri are actually moths. By analyzing all possibly identified lepidopteran representations, 

Evans’ initial claim of the butterfly label will be challenged, and the possibility of moths and 

butterflies existing within a synthesized visual language in Aegean art is explored. 

Due to the large precedent set by Evans in Aegean research, and the subsequent lack of 

challenges to even his more minor assertions, this chapter aims to provide a novel perspective 

into the analysis of lepidoptera in Aegean art. Widening the possible interpretations of the 

artwork explored here, and the many related concepts and associations present within the 

available material culture, allows for new scholarship unbound to antiquated assumptions and 

conventions. The insects within the Flotilla Fresco will be referred to as moths throughout this 

chapter, while the other outlined examples will use the generic term “lepidoptera(ns),” providing 

the space for more nuanced butterfly/moth identification within the wider corpus. 

39 The Lepidopterans of the Flotilla Fresco 

The upper register of Room 5, which contains the Miniature Fresco program, likely 

depicted a longer narrative moving across the entire room, ending with the Flotilla Fresco and 

the return to Akrotiri, providing a grand visual experience for any viewers. Within the Flotilla 

Fresco, there are five moths illustrated in specific locations: one on the prow of ship 1, two on 

the mast of ship 2, and two on the prow of ship 2 (Fig. 27.1-3). The prow moths are yellow in 

color with some red pigment showing potential detail work while the two on the mast of ship 2 

are primarily red with some yellow peeking through; this could be a case of layering pigments of 

lime to achieve different color mixing with the lower layers coming through due to wear. All 

figures have a dark outline, likely the blue-black used throughout the fresco. The moths are quite 

large respective to the other figures and structures in the fresco; they appear alike in size to birds 

similarly used as prow decoration, among other comparisons. All of the moths have “eyes” in 

their wings, large bodies, and large antennae with a notable curl at the end. The two moths on the 

prow of ship 2 showcase a differing wing design, with the wings having scalloped margins rather 

than the round margins of other moths. Additionally, the prow moths of both ships 1 and 2 are 

represented similar to the neighboring star motifs as fixtures on the physical ship, with posts 

attaching the moths to the prow. Other ships in the fleet have similar decorations of other 

animals, such as birds. 

Room 5 is the principal source for moth depictions in Theran art, as it is likely that the 

residents of Akrotiri, having time to take their valuables and leave prior to the eruption, removed 

other examples similar to the following cases found elsewhere in the Aegean. Akrotiri and its 

residences , originally excavated in 1967 by Spyridon Marinatos, have had many differing 

interpretations on the imagery and larger context of the frescoes. Analysis of relevant material 

40 finds are often outdated to newer discoveries and scholarship (Sorenson, Friedrich, and Soholm 

2019, 47).  The West House is a special case of impeccable preservation, allowing the frescoes to 

be assessed at face-value in combination with other available material, unlike fresco 

reconstructions at other sites. A good comparison demonstrating this discrepancy is the Priest-

King fresco from Knossos compared to the north-wall Fisherman Fresco in Room 5 of the West 

House; the former contains a total of nine fragments of which the arrangement and restoration 

has been debated due to the seemingly endless combination of features, whereas the north-wall 

Fisherman Fresco was discovered nearly completely intact, having slid down the wall as a sheet 

and only sustaining damage to the feet (Shaw 2004, 69; Marinatos 1974, 36). 

Depictions of Lepidoptera in Minoan Art 

As the current evidence from Akrotiri of this moth motif is from the Flotilla fresco, other, 

more naturally abandoned sites provide other mediums in which the moth presents itself. This 

additional pictorial evidence comes mainly from Crete and its many palatial sites, as well as the 

mainland city of Mycenae, primarily in the form of seal stones. Rarer are examples made of 

precious metals and materials, as well as surviving fresco fragments from less well-preserved 

sites. This motif is primarily contained within the Aegean and mainland Greece, maintaining a 

small, regional significance.  Starting in Crete with the site of Ayia Triada, known to be a major 

economic center close to the coast of the Libyan Sea, multiple seal stones depicting lepidoptera 

were found (Fig. 28.1-3) (Burke 2005, 407).  These seal stones employ many similar stylistic 

choices in the Flotilla Fresco moths when depicting these insects: forewings with either a round 

or scalloped margin and some symbol that represents an eye on both wings. The seals present a 

variety of body shapes and sizes, and one seal has straight antennae instead of curled. Seal 1 

41 specifically has semi-circular lines connecting the forewings to the body, implying hindwings 

without a proper set of them (Fig. 28.1). 

Similarly, from Archanes, a palatial site in Northern Crete near Knossos later destroyed 

by earthquakes related to the eruption of Thera, there is a gold signet ring depicting a cult scene 

with two lepidopterans on the left side (Fig. 29) (Sapouna-Sakellarakis 2003). One moth, in 

frontal view, has two antennae that do not end in a curl, a large segmented body, and two 

forewings. The other, in profile, has two thin forewings, no antennae, and a long, thin, segmented 

body. Moving back to the south of Crete, at the site of Phaistos, a palatial site similarly destroyed 

by Theran earthquakes, a double axe head was found with an incised lepidoptera in addition to a 

gold plate with two lepidopterans (Fig. 30-31) (Levi 1964, 1). The double axe head example is 

similar to many other lepidopterans mentioned, having a scalloped margin, only forewings, 

curled antennae, and “eyes” decorating the wings. The gold plate’s imagery is much more 

figurative than literal, with the two insects depicted mirroring each other perfectly and the wing 

margins having a very rigid shape. These large palatial sites, exemplary of the interconnectivity 

of Crete with the wider Aegean, p rovide a vast corpus of lepidopterans in addition to those from 

other Cretan settlements and maritime connection points. 

Seven of these insects come from Knossos. First excavated in the early 1900s, the palatial 

site of Knossos, containing gargantuan, labyrinthine structures and countless finds, was quickly 

established as a major political and economic Minoan center (Shaw 2004, 65). The Priest-King 

fresco in the South Front of the Late Minoan phase of the palace, while having many 

restorations, has, in one instance, been restored as the “King of the Lilies,” with lilies growing 

around his waist and a lepidoptera under his left arm (Fig. 32). This restoration, created by Evans 

sometime between 1926 and 1936, utilizes a fresco fragment found  in situ  that depicts a 

42 “butterfly” with seemingly three sets of wings ending in a point with two dots, a long body, and 

two antennae curving inward. The details were preserved through a sketch made by Evans and 

later donated to the Ashmolean museum (Fig. 33). According to the sketch, the wings alternate 

yellow, blue, yellow in color. The body of the insect is blue, the antennae are yellow, and the dots 

decorating the wings are red. There are no additional images of this specific fresco fragment, so 

the Ashmolean sketch and restoration are the only basis of attributing color context to this insect. 

As the only other fresco example of a lepidopteran, the similarities to the Flotilla Fresco moths 

can not be understated. Both depictions primarily use yellow as the key color for the wings and 

have exaggerated, curled antennae. The smooth shape of the wings from the Knossian example 

matches the smooth, rounded wings of the moths on the mast of Ship 2 in the Flotilla Fresco, and 

both feature similarly thin, long bodies with no segmentation. The lepidopteran’s presence within 

this fresco indicates that more were likely present in other frescoes at Knossos, but the highly 

fragmentary nature of the fresco fragments diminishes their survival, as already discussed in the 

case of the Priest-King. 

Along with this fresco fragment, multiple seal stones found at Knossos depict 

lepidopterans as the principal subject, as well as alongside dragonflies. Many of the Knossian 

lepidopterans have distinctive upper wings with swooping, semi-circular lines joining the bottom 

of the wings to the main body as either a type of hind wing or connection, similar to seal 1 from 

Ayia Triada (Fig. 34.1-6; Fig. 28.1). All of these insects feature “eyes” or eye-esque designs on 

their wings with a range of body shapes and designs; some are depicted with heavily segmented 

bodies and others are one continuous shape. One seal, currently at the Ashmolean museum, 

depicts a waterbird, an argonaut, and a lepidopteran the last of which has many of the same 

43 features as the other seals—the forewings connected to the body with semi-circular lines, long, 

curved antennae, a segmented body—but is lacking the key “eye” motif in the wings (Fig. 34.1). 

Another seal depicts three lepidopterans (two fully visible and one slightly obscured) 

entwined into a pinwheel shape, with the ends of their bodies forming the center (Fig. 34.2). One 

is seen from the frontal view while the other two are in profile. These three have mostly 

continuous bodies, wings in a tear-drop shape with additional wings behind, and have a spiked 

margin along the bottom of the wing, either as the bottom of the forewing or as the hindwing. 

Along with maintaining the eye motif on their wings, these insects display movement through 

the positioning of their antennae, most apparent with the lepidoptera in frontal view; the left 

antennae does not curl, instead moving to the side and unfurling into a straight line, while the 

right antennae, maintaining its curl, moves leftward, leaning towards center-line of the figure. 

The antennae of the other wholly visible insect follows this direction of movement. At Knossos, 

the use of lepidopteran imagery would likely have been very influential to the rest of Crete and 

surrounding Aegean due to the city’s affluence and significance. 

The site of Kato Zakros is a  Late Minoan I  (ca. 1700-1460 BCE)  settlement sitting on the 

far eastern coast of Crete containing a palatial structure, ample trade evidence, and indication of 

substantial wealth through tits Treasury of the Shrine room (Platon 1971,  238, 240, 133 ). Within 

this treasury, excavators found numerous examples of luxury goods such as marble, alabaster, 

Egyptian vessels, and ivory sculpture, including an ivory model of a lepidoptera (Fig. 35) (Platon 

1971, 148). This insect, a three-dimensional figure displaying a two-dimensional image, is 

distinctly different from the other depictions found throughout Crete, having a bifurcated body 

with the lower half ending in a point, its arms held together in a praying pose, and distinct, 

outlined eyes. More important is the wing shape which indicates both the fore and hind wings of 

44 the insect without a clear division between them, and it has a gentle, scalloped margin with both 

ends coming into points. There is a sliver of the second, far wing visible, indicating a fuller 

three-dimensionality that is not present in the figure. Two circles reminiscent of typical wing 

“eyes” puncture through the ivory, leaving two holes in the visible wing that allow one to see 

through to the other side. The figure does appear to have been made with antennae. 

Zakros has also been the source for multiple seal stones with lepidopteran features (Fig. 

36.1-4). These seal stones do not depict any lepidopterans directly, electing to instead depict 

various creatures with lepidopteran wings very similar to those on the prow of ship 2 in the 

Flotilla Fresco at the West House. These figures’ wings feature the spiked margin and the “eyes” 

seen in many depictions, but do not display any other established features. One seal resembles 

the front-facing view of a moth, with the head, (two sets of) antennae, and fuzzy legs following 

the same general positioning of a moth (Fig. 36.1). The tongue is quite elaborate and decorative, 

reminiscent of how a moth tongue coils starting at the tip, and the lepidoptera is situated in front 

of a flower that peers out between the wings. The wings also follow the scalloped edge style with 

small rosettes taking the place of the eye motif. The unique usage of the moth motif in Zakros, a 

site highly isolated from the rest of Crete, displays the localization of the motif to better suit the 

needs of those using it as well as the potential reach of influence Knossos had on the island. 

In the shaft graves of Mycenae, on mainland Greece, more depictions exist of this 

potential moth motif, specifically made out of precious metals used in grave goods. Originally 

excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 in an attempt to find the graves of Agamemnon and 

other Homeric figures (Dickenson 1976, 161-162). The first example is a gold balance with 

lepidopterans on either weighing plate (Fig. 37). These lepidopterans are more similar to the 

Zakros model example in the shape of the wings, with a scalloped margin and no clear eye motif. 

45 The head has distinct eyes and a pointed snout, and the antennae appear to source from the 

“neck” rather than the head of the insect. The second is a gold figure of a lepidoptera, with 

antennae pointing to either side and ending in a curl, circles in the wings, and scalloped margins; 

the entire figure composing an image reminiscent of an owl’s face (Fig. 38). Both lepidopterans 

have segmented bodies and a detailed thorax tapering into a point. Though the examples are few, 

these two representations are quite distinct in their find spot at Mycenae and similarity to others 

found on Crete. Due to the status associated with Cretan goods and Minoan culture as a whole, it 

is likely that these goods were imported from Crete, placing them in a similar production context 

as the examples found directly on the island. Other Minoan goods discovered in the shaft graves 

include faience vessels imported from Crete, a technique already established in Chapter I to be a 

major Minoan luxury export (Foster 2015, 298). Mycenaeans importing luxury goods with 

lepidopteran imagery indicates the motif held wealthy associations, which is compounded by 

their presence in the seal stones, signet rings, and frescoes already explored, all of which are 

generally luxury materials used by the elite. 

Additional evidence may be found in the Ring of Nestor, discovered on the southwestern 

coast of the Peloponnese near Pylos, which depicts a scene containing lepidopterans in the upper 

left quadrant of the image (Fig. 1). 4 The ring itself is only 3.5 by 2.2 cm, making the 

lepidopterans incredibly small compared to the Archanes’ signet ring, which is similar in size but 

has much more prominent lepidopterans. These two lepidopterans are very similar in style to 

those found on the ring from Archanes, as well as appearing in a similar cultic scene of 

elaborately dressed women conversing with raised arms. Evans, in his initial description of the 

ring, was incredibly confident in the identification of these figures as butterflies due to the

The various characteristics of these lepidopteran depictions present an interesting case for 

moths and butterflies existing within iconography as one symbol. This is not to suggest that the 

people of the Bronze Age Aegean were unaware of the two insects being entirely different, 

simply to present the information pointing towards a unified visual language blending 

characteristics of the two different species into one recognizable figure. The primary “moth” 

feature are the “eyes” present on the wings of the majority of examples. Though some butterfly 

species in the region have similar spots on their wings, prominent wing “eyes” are generally 

associated with moths (Coutsis 1997, 582). The presence of only forewings is indicative of 

neither insect specifically; however, the rounded shape of the forewing can be attributed to both 

insects and does not favor one over the other. The scalloped wing margins can also represent 

both, but is generally attributed to various butterfly species (582). The various antennae also 

show a blending of characteristics, as both curved, curled, and straight antennae are observed. It 

is important to note that curled antennae as depicted do not occur solely in butterflies, as they 

occur in some moth families like the  Crambidae , and that the association of curled antennae with 

butterflies is primarily a modern one. These three antennae shapes can apply to both species, as 

47 moth and butterfly antennae exist on a range of straight to curled, and the defining features of 

“clubbed” versus “hair-like” are not present within these representations (NCMNS 2021). 

The body shapes and sizes also similarly apply to both animals, as the variety of long and 

short, thin and stout, bifurcated and continuous bodies is representative of both moths and 

butterflies (NCMNS 2021). All of these features combine to create a vaguely lepidopteran motif, 

not being clearly one or the other. This does not apply to all insects within Aegean art, as 

dragonflies appear clearly as themselves in multiple instances (Coutsis 1997, 580). As this 

phenomenon applies to lepidopterans specifically, it points towards a synthesis of the visual 

language surrounding the insects that provide grounds for further analysis to determine the exact 

identity of each representation. The presence of a generalized “lepidopteran” motif does not 

inherently negate a specific identity, rather establishing that assumptions cannot be made solely 

off of their appearance and must take into consideration the cultural and physical context 

surrounding it, as was explored in the previous chapter. 

The lepidoptera/moth motif found throughout Minoan and Minoan-influenced art is 

incredibly prolific, with multiple instances of it cropping up throughout various art mediums and 

contexts. A clear preference for this motif appearing in higher-end materials, such as precious 

metals, ivory, and frescoes, indicates a prestigious context for its appearance. Those shown in the 

Flotilla Fresco are simultaneously unique within their maritime context and part of a wider 

phenomenon using these insects to represent various aspects of Minoan culture. These aspects, 

further explored after an inspection of the economic and cultural context that this motif existed 

and proliferated in, allow for a deeper understanding of the purposes and uses of the lepidopteran 

motif and its association with many key aspects of Minoan-influenced Aegean society. 

48 Associations Between Commerce, Textiles, and the Sea 

In addition to the pictorial references, further indication of moths as part of Theran life 

and economy lies within their husbandry and commercial practices displayed through the 

archaeological and literary record. In Panagiotakopulu et al. (1997), the original proposal of the 

lepidoptera depicted being moths rather than butterflies, their theory centers around the find of a 

calcified silk cocoon near surrounding structures of the House of the Ladies, a building just north 

of the West House (Fig. 39) (420). This cocoon is likely to be from the moth  Pachypasa otis , a 

silk moth known to have been used in later periods to imitate Chinese silk imports (Fig. 40) 

(422). Another silk moth species known from later periods,  Saturnia pyri , or Giant Peacock 

Moth, follows the pictorial representations previously established more closely; these moths have 

“eyes” on all four wings to deter predation, as well as being generally brown in color and 

incredibly large (Fig. 41). A gemstone from a later period, dated to the 1 st  century BCE, displays 

lepidoptera very similar to the  Saturnia pyri , having the shorter, pointy antennae of moths, a 

thicker, short body, and all four wings displayed (Fig. 42). This moth is accompanied by both a 

chrysalis, in the shape of a typical moth silk cocoon, and a caterpillar, with all of the body 

segments typical of a  Saturnia pyri  caterpillar. This species is widespread across Europe, while 

the aforementioned  Pachypasa otis  has a more narrow home range, spreading from Italy to the 

Levant (422). Though  Pachypasa otis  is not known to be native to Santorini, there is a high 

likelihood that the cocoon was imported from elsewhere in the Aegean, specifically the islands of 

Kos or Amorgos, due to Akrotiri’s affluence in maritime trade and commerce (Panagiotakopulu 

1997, 586). 

Following this thread of insect cultivation is the presence of beekeeping in the Bronze 

Age Aegean as a practice that similarly found its way into art through jewelry, seal stones, and 

49 frescoes. Apiculture was performed throughout the Aegean from the Protopalatial period into the 

Late Minoan on both Crete and Akrotiri, Thera (Brandon 2025, 226). It is potentially depicted 

within the Flotilla Fresco of the West house, with an apiary featured in the complex background 

of the procession scene in the town the flotilla is sailing towards, according to Irini 

Papageorgiou’s interpretation (Papageorgiou 2016, 103). Additionally, early interpretations of 

some vessels excavated by Marinatos include ceramic basins as beehives, as well as some other, 

smaller vessels thought to be smaller beehives (258). Further assessment of the presence of 

beekeeping on Crete at the site of Sissi occurred through the combined effort of excavation of 

pottery remains and organic residue analysis testing for the presence of lipids sourced from bee 

products, namely beeswax (120). The  Gold Pendant in the Shape of Two Facing Bees , housed at 

the Heraklion Museum on Crete, shows how bees were represented within Minoan art: long, 

pointed wings with segmented bodies and very distinct eyes (Fig. 43). 5 Moth cultivation would 

likely have been less institutionalized than honeybee cultivation, as modern wild-silk practices 

involve gathering the silk cocoons from trees where the silkworms naturally gather, and would 

thus have very little archaeological presence (McKinney and Eicher 2009, 51). 

Tangential to the cultivation of various insects for their by-products is the production of 

mollusk-sourced goods, namely sea-silk from the mussel  Pinna nobilis  and the well known 

Tyrian purple dye from murex snails. Murex dye is known to have been produced all over the 

Aegean, with production sites at Akrotiri, Aegina Kolonna, multiple locations on Crete, Rhodes, 

and outside the Aegean along the Eastern Mediterranean coast. These identifications are based on 

archaeological finds such as discarded murex shells, pottery that previously housed the pigment, 

and blocks of unused pigment (Sotiropoulou et al. 2021, 172-173; Berger et al. 2024, 4). The
